en: Oṃ, homage to Vighnavināyaka!
I bow to the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world—
the Lord of the Universe, the Sustainer of the Universe, who is the Universe itself and the Cause of the Universe.
The seed of the world, whose nature is truth, the witness of all, the imperishable,
the omniscient, dwelling within all beings, the all-powerful, the pervasive Lord.
Having paid homage to the Brahmins by the command of the King of Navadvīpa,
[I shall describe] the origin of the Brahmins together with their divisions and so forth,
as well as the *gotra*, *gāṇa*, and *samanvita* lineages of the noble lords of Rāḍhā.
That account of the king's life is called the *Vallālacarita*.
Pulaha was born from the left ear of Brahmā as he desired to create;
Aṅgiras was born from the cavity of his nostrils, and Ruci from his mouth.
Marīci emerged from the region of the shoulders, Pracetas from the lower lip,
and the eleven Rudras, born of wrath, from the forehead.
Vātsya was the son of Pulaha, and Śāṇḍilya was the son of Ruci;
Āṅgirasa was the son of Bṛhaspati, and Bharadvāja is recorded as his son. Kaśyapa, the progenitor (Prajāpati), was born from the mind of Marīci.
From Pracetas was born the venerable sage Gautama of the mind.
Sāvarṇi was born from Gautama; he indeed was a preeminent sage. There were five gotras among them, and these were their pravaras.
O King, other Brahmin castes arose from the mouth of Brahmā;
they remain distinct according to their different regions and are devoid of [specific] lineages (gotras).
Kaśyapa begot the twelve Ādityas upon Aditi;
and from the impurity of Atri’s eye, the Moon indeed arose in the Ocean of Milk.
The foremost Kṣatriyas are remembered as being descended from Candra, Āditya, and Manu;
other Kṣatriya lineages likewise arose from the region of Brahmā’s arms.
From the region of his thighs came the Vaiśyas, and from his feet the Śūdra castes.
By birth one is born a Śūdra; by sacramental rites one is called a Dvija;
by the study of the Vedas one becomes a Vipra; and by the knowledge of Brahman one is a Brāhmaṇa.
The Sarasvatas, Kānyakubjas, Gauḍas, Maithilas,
and Kolkalas are declared to be the five Gauḍas who dwell to the north of the Vindhya mountains.
The Karṇāṭas, the Tailaṅgas, the Gurjjaras who dwell in the kingdom,
the Andhras, and the five Draviḍas are those who inhabit the south of the Vindhya mountains.
All the twice-born ones from Kānyakubja, with the exception of those from Mathurā and Magadha, are [so called].
Māgadha was fashioned as a Brahmin by Brahmā at the beginning of the Kalpa;
likewise, through the heat of Varāha, one is born as a Māthura.
In Gauḍa, at the time marked by the Vedas, arrows, and the elephant goad (459), the Brahmins assembled;
all of them were experts in every scripture, having mounted horse-drawn vehicles.
Among them were Medhātithi, Kṣitīśa, Vītarāga, and Suṣeṇaka.
And likewise the sage Saubhari, Ratnagarbha, and Sudhānidhi.
By the king's command, seven hundred sons were borne by them;
through the power of that deity, seven excellent sons were born among them.
Five went to Varaṇāra, while the youngest remained in Rāḍha.
The group of five Brahmins was brought by the king of men, Ādiśūra;
their names and lineages, belonging to five clans, are now being told.
Bharadvāja is recorded as the lineage of Śrīharṣa; Kāśyapa is remembered for Dakṣa; Sāvarṇa for Vedagarbha; Vātsya for Chāndasika;
and the lineage of Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa is said to be Śāṇḍilya.
Sixteen were born from Bhaṭṭa, and sixteen also from Dakṣa;
four were born from Śrīharṣa, upholders of the Bharadvāja lineage;
twelve from Vedagarbha, and likewise eleven from Chāṇḍaḍa.
Some Brahmins arrived who were Vedic scholars and masters of the Vedas;
those from the west and the south are remembered as the Śeṣas, while the Draviḍas are also mentioned.
Regarding Ballāla, the gods themselves are surely his kinsmen;
those learned in the Vedas are to be known as Merus, and the panegyrists as water-jars. (Valc 1.23)
Conduct, discipline, knowledge, stability, visiting sacred fords,
completion of one's duties, austerity, and charity— these are the nine characteristics of a noble family.
A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father's house until death;
yet he must never give her in marriage to one of low birth.
Having studied a single Vedic branch together with its ritual manuals, or having mastered the six auxiliary sciences, [one becomes a teacher].
A Brahmin devoted to the six duties, learned in the Vedas, is called a knower of dharma.
In accordance with his virtues, the king Vallāla long ago firmly established him as a man of noble birth, an original member of the lineage, and one born of a pure descent. (Valc 1.27)
Thus ends the account of the origin of the castes in the *Vallālacarita*.
Now follows the explanation of the reasons for the designation of recipients (*pratigrāhin*).
The king bestowed a golden cow upon the Brahmins at the sacrifice.
He fell while cutting that cow made of gold.
Then, O Brahmins, a certain goldsmith was banished by the king; others were born from the acceptance of gifts and became excluded from all religious duties.
Thus ends the section on the recipient's causes.
Now follow the names of those designated as recipients, along with their villages:
Śaṅkara, Pītamuṇḍī, Gaḍa, and Divākara.
Guda, the one named Dāḍaka, Dokaḍi, and Pippalī. Valc 1.30.
The one named Mārttaṇḍa was a venerable Brāhmaṇa by name;
Āyāni, Gaṇāyi, Hāḍa, and Gopī were born of Vandin.
Māṣa, Dokaḍi by name, Rāya, and Madhusūdana [were also there].
Kuśika, Yavana by name, Haḍa, and Nārāyaṇa as well.
Mahinta, Dividha by name, Dāvāri, and Keśava; Caṭṭa, named Śakuni, and Nayārika from Tailavāṭī. Valc 1.33.
Kunda was named Viśveśvara, and his younger brother was known as Viṭhu; these two brothers, born of Ghoṣā, were Madana and Viśvarūpa.
Gāṅguli, Hāsyanāman, Pūti known as Gautama,
the one named Parāśara, Śimlī, Śaṅkara, and the one called Ḍiṇḍi—
these twice-born men, born of brahmin families, accepted the gift of cows.
By the mere connection with them, one sinks like a cow in the mud.
In matters of relationship, at a meal, in giving, and likewise in sacrifice,
as well as during the time of a śrāddha rite, these should be avoided again and again by the wise.
Thus end the names and other details of the recipients. Now follows the description of the marriages of the sons of the recipients:
the daughters of Gaṇaka were given to Vasiṣṭha, and the daughters of Śakuni to Ṭoṭa.
Kubera is the giver of daughters, and he is the lord of laughter.
Cakrapāṇi also took a maiden out of greed for wealth;
and Caṭṭaja, becoming the husband of Viṭhu’s daughter, was the ornament of his lineage.
These six are remembered as the progenitors of the family through the marriage of the adopted son. (Valmīki-vamśāvalī 1.39)
Having given his daughter to one learned in the Vedas, a man of noble birth is once again born into his lineage.
Having obtained the village from Vallāla, Kauṇḍilya was established there;
likewise Yavagrāmī, Kaḍāra, Kauṇḍilya, and Vaiduḍī.
Thus concludes the account of the marriages of the sons of Pratigrāhin.

Next follows the account of the names and other details of those belonging to the five *gotras*. Then follow the names of the *gāms* (lineages) of the descendants of Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa of the Śāṇḍilya *gotra*.
First, Varāha should be saluted; then Rāma, Gaḍagi, Nṛpa, Keśara, Nāna, and Kusumakaulika.
Vāṭu would be Pārihāla, named Kulabhigu;
he attained the status of a Gaṇa among the Ghoṣalins, as did Seyu and Śāṇḍīśvara. (Valc 1.43)
Vuḍoma and Caraka, Vaṭavyāla and Vikartana,
Vasurāyi as well as Nīla, Kaḍyāla and Madhusūdana.
Kuśī, Koyanāman, Kulisā, Vāsuka, Ākāśa, Mādhava, Dīrghagrāmī, and Mahāmati. Valc 1.45.
These sixteen Śāṇḍilyas have been described, honored by kings;
thereafter, the lineage of Dakṣa belonging to the Kāśyapa gotra is told.
Now, the names of those belonging to the Gāmin lineage, who are the upholders of the lineage of Dakṣa of the Kāśyapa gotra:
Dhīra will be the lord of Guḍīgrāma; Nīra will be the lord of Āmarūlika; Bhūriṣṭāla will be Śubha; and Śambhu will be the lord of Tailavāṭika.
Kautuka is Pītamuṇḍī; Caṭṭagrāmī is Sulocana;
Palaśāyin is named Pālu; and likewise, Haḍḥkāka is considered [to be] so.
Poḍāri is known as Kṛṣṇa; Pāladhi is named Rāma;
Jananāman is Koyāri; and Parkkaṭi is Vanamālika.
Simalāyī Śrīhari, Jaṭa, Pūṣalika,
Bhaṭṭagrāmī Śaśidhara, and Mūlagrāmī Keśava—
these sixteen should be known as the Brahmanas belonging to the Kāśyapa lineage.
Now, the names of the descendants of Śrī Harṣa of the Bharadvāja lineage are as follows:
Dhāṃdu by name shall be Mukhaiṭi; Jana shall be Dīnasāyika;
Nāna is to be known as Sāharika; and Rāyī shall be named Rāma. (Valc 1.51)
These sons of Śrīharṣa, born of the lineage of Bharadvāja,
are known throughout all lands as the four foremost leaders.
Now, the names of those of the Gāmi clan, who maintain the lineage of Vedagarbha of the Sāvarṇa gotra:
Gāṅgulī, Halanāman, Kunda, Rājyadhara, Vasiṣṭha, Siddhala, Dāyin, and Madana are to be known [as the teachers]. Valc 1.53.
Viśvarūpa, Nandin, Vāligrāmin, Kumāraka, the yogin Siyārika, Puṃsika, and the one named Rāma are to be known [as such]. (Valc 1.54)
Dakṣa, known as Sākaṭa, Pārī, Madhusūdana,
Ghaṇṭāgrāmī, Mādhava, and Nāyārī, who is Guṇākara—
these twelve sons of great wisdom are remembered as the Sāvarṇas.
Now, the names of the lineage-holders of the Vātsya *gotra* among the Chāndasas are:
Ravi, Mahintā, Surabhi, Ghoṣa, Kavi, Śimbalāla on earth, Mahāyaśas, Vāpulika, Piplī, Dhīra, Pūti, and indeed the one named Śaṅkara. (Valc 1.56)
Viśvaṃbhara was indeed the chief of Pūrvagrāma, and the Vātsyas were the people whose dwelling place was for that purpose.
Śrī Śrīdhara was indeed Kāñjivillī, and he named Nārāyaṇa was Kāñjiyārī;
Guṇākara was Cautkhaṇḍika, and Mano Dīghāla was equal to Rudra on earth. (Valc 1.57)
Now follows the enumeration of those belonging to the secondary lineages (*gauṇakulīna*):
Dīrghāṅgī, Pāri, Kulabhī, Poḍārī, Rāi, Keśarī,
Ghaṇṭā, Ḍiṇḍi, Pītamuṇḍī, Mahintā, and Guḍpippalī.
Haḍha and gaḍgaḍi—these are proclaimed as secondary (gauṇa) [qualities]. Hereafter, that which is the specific distinction in this very context shall be described by me.
Once, in order to establish his noble lineage, the king’s favorite invited Brahmins to the ceremony of ascending the assembly hall.
Having performed their daily rites, on the day determined for that purpose,
all the brahmins arrived in the assembly hall in the presence of the king.
Some went into the presence of the king within one watch, some within one and a half watches, and others within two and a half watches.
Then the wise king, having discerned the actions of the twice-born, [proceeded].
There, he joyfully bestowed upon them noble lineage and other such qualities as were appropriate.
When one and a half *praharas* had passed, those twice-born who had come to the assembly— being fully established in the Dharma— attained noble lineage.
Those śrotriyas who arrive within one and a half watches (prahara) are proclaimed [as such];
those who have arrived within the interval of a watch (yāma), however, belong to the secondary lineage (gauṇakulīna).
In due course, they were established among the pure *śrotriyas* who were the original [recipients],
and they became renowned as the "secondary" (*gauṇa*) ones, known by the designation of "hard-to-find *śrotriyas*" (*kaṣṭa-śrotriya*).
"Just as those who are secondary are difficult [to deal with], so too must those who are base be abandoned at all times.
Thus was the determination of the lineage declared by the Brahmins of Rāḍha.
Thus ends the account of the Brahmins of Rāḍha regarding their attainment of noble lineage and other qualities. Now follows the account of the Varendra lineage:
eighteen [gotras] are to be known among the Kāśyapas, and fourteen among the Śāṇḍilyas.
There are twenty-four [gotras] of the Vātsyas, and likewise among the Bharadvājas.
In the Sāvarṇi [Manvantara], twenty [sages] belonging to five lineages (*gotra*) are to be known;
their villages are now described in detail and in due order.
Now, the names of the villages of those who uphold the lineage of the compassionate treasury, the one of the Kāśyapa *gotra*: Valc_1.68. [[011]]
Karañja, bhāduḍī, maitra, bālayaṣṭika, kerala, madhugrāmī, balīhārī, moyālī, and bījakuñjaka. (Valc 1.69)
Koṭi, Sarvagrāmakoṭi, Pareśa, Dhosaka,
Bhadrayāmī, Aśrukoṭi, the renowned Śaragrāmī, Velagrāmī, Camagrāma, and those born of the lineage of the Treasure of Compassion. Valc 1.70.
Now, the names of the Gāmins who uphold the lineage of Dāmodara of the Śāṇḍilya gotra are as follows:
Rudravāgcin, Sādhuvāgcin, Lāhiḍi, Campaṭi, Nandanāvāṭī, Kālindī, Caṭṭagrāmī, and Pūṣaṇa. (Valc 1.71)
Śihari, Viśī, Matsyāśī, Veluḍī, the one named Campa,
and Suvarṇatoṭa were born in the lineage of Śāṇḍilya and Udāmodara.
Now, the names of the lineage-holders of the Vātsya clan, the Dharādharas:
Saṃyāminī, Bhīmakālī, Bhaṭṭaśālī, and Kuḍmuḍi;
Bhāḍiyāla, Kāmakālī, Vātsyagrāmī, and Lakṣaka. Valc_1.73. [[012]]
Voḍgrāma, Jāmarūkha, Kālīgrāma, and Kalīhara.
Śītalī, Dhosalī, Tāluḍī, Kukkuṭī,
Nidrālī, Cākṣuṣagrāmī, Deulī, and Sihaṛī.
Prauṇḍrīkākṣi, Śrutavaṭī, Caturāndī,
and likewise Kālindī are known as the descendants of Dharādhara of the Vātsya lineage.
Now, the names of the descendants of Gautama of the Bharadvāja lineage who uphold the family line:
Bhādaḍa, Lāḍḍela, Jhāmā, Jhāmālī, and Jhampaṭī; also Urttivāhī, Ugrarekhī, Ākhu, Ratnābalī, and Khani. (Valc 1.70)
Gosvāśirā, atha, pisvīni, ceṅgā, cākhuri, pippalī,
viśālā, kāñcanagrāmī, asṛk, and likewise śākoṭaka.
Kṣetragrāmī, Rājagrāmī, Nandīgrāmī, and Jadhyala;
Pūkti and Bṛhatī among the lineages, from Gotama among the Bharadvājas.
Now, the names of the Gāmins who uphold the lineage of Parāśara of the Sāvarṇa gotra:
Siṃhaḍālaka, Unduḍī, Śṛṅgī, Pākaḍī, Ledhuḍī, Dhundhuḍī, Tātoyā, Setu, Kapālī, and Lomapeṭarau. (Valc 1.80) [[013]]
Pañcavaṭī, Khaṇḍavaṭī, Nikaṭa, and Samudraka;
Puṇḍarika, Yaśogrāma, and the renowned Ketugrāma.
Puṣpapā, Bhāduṣi, Varendra, and those known as Gāmi—
these were born from Parāśara during the Sāvarṇa periods, being equal to sages.
Now, as for the reason why the Vaidikas were devoid of Kaulinī and other [qualifications]:
the Vaidika Brāhmaṇas had become partisans of the merchants;
consequently, the lord of the earth, out of anger, did not summon them to the assembly.
"O ascetics rich in austerity, some Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda and follow the Vedas do not desire the offerings bestowed by the king. Valmiki Ramayana 1.84.
Thus ends the statement regarding the lack of noble lineage (*kaulīnya*) and other qualities among the Vaidikas.
Now follow the names and lineages (*gotra*) of those belonging to the Kanyakubja region:
born in the *Kāśyapa* lineage was the highly intelligent one named Dakṣa.
His servant was Daśaratha Vasu, born of the Gautama lineage.
Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa was born in the Śāṇḍilya lineage;
his pupil was Ghoṣaja Makarandaka, the servant of Saubhāgila.
Among the Bharadvājas, the most excellent sage Śrīharṣa is renowned;
his servant was named Virāṭa, and Guhaka is remembered as a descendant of Kaśyapa. He is designated as belonging to the Sāvarṇa lineage, a treasury of the Vedas whose wealth is asceticism.
His servant was one of the Mitravaṃśa lineage, belonging to the Gotra of Viśvāmitra;
he was known as Kālidāsa and was born of a Śūdra family.
Born in the Vātsya lineage and known as Chāṇḍaḍa,
and born in the Maudgalya lineage and named Datta Puruṣottama—
for the protection of these, Svāgata [came] to the Gauḍha region. (Valc 1.89)
Ghoṣa, Vasu, Mitra, and all those of noble lineage—
Devadatta, Senasiṃha, Pālita, Kara, Guha,
and Dāsa— these eight were the middling ones; thereafter came seventy-two villages.
The eighty original families approved by Rājavallālasena,
and those seventy-two households— these are recorded as the lowest among the scribes (kāyasthas).
Now, the praise of virtuous scribes:
"But those Śūdras who are devoted to giving, endowed with vows, and dedicated to the Brahmins—their food is always fit to be well-eaten; this was seen by the ancient twice-born. (Valc 1.92)
Thus ends the first section of the *Vallālacarita* as narrated by Ānandabhaṭṭa.
[015] The *Vallālacarita*, Second Section.
Now begins the first chapter: "The history of Vallāla in its former section has been narrated by me;
now listen, as it is being told in detail in the latter section. (Valc 2.1.1)
The renowned King Vallāla, a bearer of the Sena lineage,
protected this city and the earth with his power and unimpaired command.

And although the lord was in the prime of youth, he possessed discernment; never did the king take a Brahmin maiden as his wife. Though he acted according to his desires and was proud, he remained a servant to Priyaṅkara.
And at no time did the king act as a paramour to the wives of others.
The king, who followed the doctrines of heretics, consorted for twelve years with a Cāṇḍāla girl and a dancer’s daughter for the sake of attaining supernatural powers.
As long as the king had not been instructed by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda,
he performed various deeds censured by the virtuous; however,
after that, by means of Vimalabuddhi, who followed the teachings of the Bhaṭṭa, [he acted otherwise].
What deed, pleasing to the brahmins, has not been performed?
Vaṅga, Vāgadā, Daṇḍivāra, Rāḍhā, and Mithilā— the earth—
constituted his vast kingdom, this pentad of provinces.
In former times, the illustrious king resided at will in the excellent city of Gauḍa,
or perhaps in the city of Vikrama.
Sometimes in the village of Svarṇagrāma, or in a most enchanting palace,
he took his pleasure with the goddesses of fortune, like the lord of the gods in heaven.
He was learned in the sciences of pleasure and skilled on horseback;
he was supremely proficient in the use of weapons and, in generosity, like another Karṇa.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction to Vallāla," in the *Vallālacarita* composed by Ānandabhaṭṭa.
Now begins the second chapter:
The lord of the earth, desiring to conquer the sovereign of Purodantapura, [set forth].
From his wealthy and beloved father-in-law, he received ten million gold coins.
Since the king had been defeated again and again in the battle at Maṇipura,
he prepared himself to launch a formidable assault.
Even though his beloved was unwilling to give it, having witnessed her transgression of their agreement,
he dispatched a messenger to that high-souled merchant.
That messenger, having approached the beloved [king] who was staying at Saṅkakoṭa,
then announced the royal decree of King Vallāla.
Vallāla said:
"Indeed, we must undertake a military expedition against Kīkaṭa,
having made a great effort and being joined by the sixfold army."
Then Vallabhacandra, receiving the letter concerning his life,
dispatched fifty million gold pieces without delay.
Vallabha said:
"The king, being excessively spendthrift, once caused Kālikā to fall;
what can we say of that monarch? I have never seen such conduct among the virtuous."
Why then this exertion for battle? It is only fitting to protect that which has been obtained; this war is without cause.
Let go of the desire for the village, out of a wish for the welfare of the subjects;
for war causes the destruction of the people, is unrighteous, and leads to hell.
A king who acts according to his own whims does not perceive the duty of kingship;
in failing to protect [his subjects], there is great fault—what merit is there in those who merely increase the kingdom?
Neither a man afflicted with a chronic disease, nor a devotee of the Blessed One, nor even a pestle or a bow— no person whatsoever is ever capable of making [these] so.
A king who collects taxes alone without protecting his subjects incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
Thus say the followers of Kauṣītaki: "O King, what is the use of debating statecraft?
For statecraft is to be understood as the crushing of enemies. (Valc 2.2.13)
Alternatively, because people like us are tormented by conflicts just as common reeds are,
for that reason I speak thus.
If the king were to grant this land of Harikeli together with the collection of taxes as a pledge,
then I would venture to repay that debt.
Having arrived at the city of Vikrama with his horses exhausted, that messenger reported all of what he had been told to Vallāla.
Having heard this message, King Vallāla then blazed with fury, like a fire-receptacle kindled by flames.
Then, from his face copper-red with anger, a stream of perspiration flowed forth,
like moisture and burning resin from fuel heated by contact with fire.
Though the merchants were innocent, Vallāla, having become enraged at his beloved and his own aged father,
wrought a terrible slaughter among them.
Under the pretext of collecting customs duties,
he forcibly seized the goods of merchants even while they were crying out in protest during their legal transactions.
Although marriage with a woman of a different caste was forbidden even in the Kali age,
he forcibly abducted the daughter of a merchant named Govindādya.
Even though Nahuṣa, the god among men, came with his family elders and repeatedly urged him from his golden throne, he did not accept it.

Once, having mounted a swift horse, the king went out at his own will.
He proceeded to the beautiful grove belonging to Dhavaleśvarī.
Wandering through delightful forests on the riverbanks and along the sandy shores, he beheld her roaming upon the river’s edge.
Her breasts were round, with prominent nipples, firm, and closely set;
she, the one with beautiful eyes, was covering them with the hem of her garment out of modesty.
She had beautiful hair and pure teeth; she was a young girl with a lotus-like face, slender-limbed, with very delicate members, a fine nose, and a gentle smile.
She was endowed with large, rounded hips, possessed beautiful cheeks, and was captivating;
accompanied by her one dear friend, she was like a lotus plant grown on dry land.
From the lotus-face of that most beloved woman,
the king’s eyes, like bees, drank the essence of her loveliness.
His body pierced by her intoxicating sidelong glances, the lord of the earth,
upon beholding her, quickly fell under the sway of the god of love.
Approaching that woman of beautiful hips, whose eyes resembled lotuses, he drew near.
Gazing at her as she stood there with unblinking eyes, he spoke these words.
The king said:
"With her eyes she surpasses the blue lotus; with her face, the lotus; with her teeth, the kunda flower; and with her lower lip, the ripe bimba fruit."
Outshining the campaka petal with your limb,
who are you, shining like a forest goddess in the grove on the riverbank?
O Kundadanti, King Vallālasena— the lotus-feet of whose feet are served by assemblies of neighboring vassals— is the cause of widowhood for other beautiful women.
Since the object to be accomplished has been presented, cast your gaze upon it, O Kuru.
Having heard that, her passion aroused, she then concealed her true feelings;
with her face slightly cast down, she spoke to the king in a soft voice.
The maiden said:
"O Lord of the Earth, do not speak thus to me, a mere girl!
Where is your lineage, descended from the Moon, and where is my own origin?"
"I am known in the world as the daughter of a leather-worker;
indeed, I am not of noble birth, so I am not fit to be married by you."
The king said:
"O girl, why do you delude me by speaking thus?
Could such a form as this belong to a leather-worker's daughter—one that is enchanting to the whole world?"
"You are not the daughter of a cobbler; he is merely your protector.
You are surely a princess, O blessed lady; of this there is no doubt."
O lady of beautiful countenance, what kind of base man would there be in this world who,
having obtained you— who are like a priceless treasure come into his hand— would cast you away?
Whether you are of noble birth or not, you alone are the beloved of my heart;
come with me, for I shall lead you to my own city.
Having heard those words of the king, she, with her eyes cast askance,
then prompted her friend to speak what was appropriate for that occasion.
The friend said:
"If you have resolved to take her hand in marriage according to the sacred rites, then lead her away with you; she gives herself to you."
The king said:
"By the Gandharva rite, she has come to me of her own accord; I am her husband, and she is the mistress of my life. (Valmiki Ramayana 2.3.20)
Having spoken thus to the daughter of the courtesan, he addressed her once more—
she who possessed a beautiful face— as his own countenance blossomed with a mass of supreme bliss.
The king said:
"Come with me; become my wife and ascend this excellent vehicle.
Be the mistress in my inner apartments and over all my harem."
Having spoken thus, he smiled and took hold of you as you were trembling;
sending your companions away by means of a vehicle, he led you to the city of Vikrama.
Then, having settled that woman of faultless limbs in his own home,
the king enjoyed her according to his desire, having lost all interest in his royal duties.
That leather-worker’s daughter was excessively pampered by the king;
she attended upon him within the inner apartments amidst the breeze of waving yak-tail fans.
Dwelling together with her who had entered the inner apartments,
the king did not perceive at all the great lapse of time that had passed.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Meeting with Sundarī," in the *Vallālacarita* as proclaimed by Ānandabhaṭṭa.

I shall do what is pleasing to him; I swear this to you by my lovely feet.

Having heard these words spoken by that Kāma, who holds others in his power,

I fall at your feet with my head; why do you not show compassion to your husband?

"For the husband is indeed the protector of women, especially of young women;

"For a woman, the husband is indeed her refuge; the husband is her supreme deity.

"Devotion to her husband is the supreme duty for women;

Unlike an ordinary woman devoid of devotion to her husband,
I always worship you, having established you upon the lotus-seat of my heart.
"By that same low conduct and wrong path through which I was constantly honored with prostrations and devotion, I have now been insulted.
Fie upon him! He is of sinful behavior, blinded by lust, and his senses are disordered."
That evil-minded man who lusts after his mother, though I am devoted to my husband.
Today, O Lord, I went to the chamber for washing the feet;
seeing me there alone, he followed after me with a smile.
O Lord, because my friend was called by me while I was terrified, she went there quickly;
therefore, she was not defiled by that evil-minded one.
"Protected by righteousness, I speak to you as is fitting;
my limbs tremble when I recall his wicked conduct."

Meditating on his son’s wicked conduct, the king, agitated by anger,

and the Itihāsas and Purāṇas were narrated out of compassion.
The treatises on dharma have been proclaimed, yet the Kali age now prevails;
even Kṛṣṇa has attained whiteness through his graying hair.
O Brahmin, O great sage, you who know the true essence of dharma, tell us today yourself this Purāṇa; for we are worthy of your grace.
We shall not abandon you without hearing the ancient tale;
for you are bound at the feet by the cords of our devotion, and you are no longer your own master.
Having heard their words, he, the best among those skilled in speech, spoke as if smiling slightly: "Listen, I shall tell you."
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Vallālacarita of the Vyāsapurāṇa.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
Having encompassed the earth on all sides, he stood beyond it by ten fingers' breadth.
From him Virāj was born; from Virāj was born Puruṣa.
Then, as he was meditating, Rudra was born from his forehead.
The moon was born from his mind; from his eye the sun was born;
from his mouth Indra and Agni were born; from his breath Vāyu was born.
The one of great splendor created the seven mind-born [sages]: Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasiṣṭha.
For the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs,
and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Whenever the creatures being created did not increase, he divided his own body in two; with one half he became a man, and with the other half a woman; in her he procreated various kinds of offspring.
Pervading both heaven and earth with their majesty, they remain;
these seven hosts of the ancestors have been described by me in the Purāṇa.
The Vairājas, the Agniṣvāttas, and likewise the Barhiṣads are remembered;
as well as the Sukālas, the Haviṣmants, the Susvadhās, and the Somapas.
Of these, the first three kings are remembered as formless ancestors (pitṛs);
together with the four beginning with Sakala, these seven are remembered as the Gaṇas.
The sons of Virāṭ are the Somasads, the Agniṣvāttas born of Marīci,
the Barhiṣads born of Pulastya, and the Sukālas born of Vasiṣṭha;
the Susvadhās were born from Pulaha, while the Somapas are the sons of Kavi.
Seeking their respective fruits, those of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes nourish the gods known as Sukālas, Haviṣmants, Susvadhās, and Somapas.
Wherein those principal hosts of the Pitṛs have been proclaimed,
their sons and grandsons also should be known to be infinite.
Viśva, Viśvabhuj, Ārādhya, Dharma, Dhanya, Śubhānana,
Bhūtida, Bhūtikṛt, and Bhūti— these are the nine hosts of the Pitṛs.
The auspicious, the maker of health, the healthy one, the refuge of those who are healthier,
the cause of health, and the faultless— these six are remembered as the groups [of qualities].
Vara, Vareṇya, Varada, Puṣṭida, Tuṣṭida,
Viśvapātṛ, and Dhātṛ— these seven are likewise the Gaṇas.
Mahān, Mahātman, Mahita, Mahimāvan, and Mahābala—
these five hosts of the ancestors are likewise destroyers of sin.
One bestows happiness, another bestows wealth, another bestows Dharma, and yet another bestows prosperity;
thus is this fourfold group of ancestors described.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Account of Creation and Emanation," in the Vallālacarita from the Vyāsapurāṇa.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Time created the Virāj; that Virāj created the Puruṣa.
Know that Puruṣa to be Manu, born from the thighs of the Virāj.
Having indeed created those subjects, that Lord of Creatures, Āpava,
the Puruṣa, obtained Śatarūpā as his wife, who was not born from a womb.
From the Puruṣa Vairāja, Śatarūpā gave birth to Vīra;
from Vīra, Kāmyā gave birth to Priyavrata and Uttānapāda.
The highly fortunate Kāmyā was the daughter of the progenitor Kardama;
and he had four sons: Samrāṭ, Kukṣi, Virāṭ, and Prabhu.
Having approached Priyavrata as her husband, she gave birth to sons;
the patriarch Atri took Uttānapāda as his son.
From Uttānapāda, Sunṛtā— renowned as the daughter of Dharma and known by the name Sunṛtā, possessed of beautiful hips— gave birth to four sons.
The auspicious mother of Dhruva was born from the horse sacrifice (Vājimedha).
And Prajāpati Uttānapāda begot Dhruva, Kīrtimant, Āyuṣmant, and Vasu upon Sunṛtā.
Through his ascetic penance, Dhruva attained the station situated before the Seven Sages;
from that Dhruva, Śambhu begot Śliṣṭi and Bhavya.
Succhāyā, through her union with Śliṣṭi, bore five stainless sons:
Ripu, Ripuñjaya, Ripra, Vṛkala, and Vṛkatejas.
Vṛhatī bore to Ripu Cākṣuṣa, who possessed all splendor;
and Cākṣuṣa begot Manu upon Puṣkariṇī Vīraṇī.
To Naḍvalā, the daughter of the high-souled Prajāpati Araṇya, ten sons of great luster were born to Manu.
O best of men, from Vairāja Prajāpati were born Kanyā,
Ūru, Puru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavāk, and Kavi.
Agniṣṭu, Atirātra, and Sudyumna— these nine,
along with Abhimanyu as the tenth, were of great prowess, born of Naḍvalā.
From her thighs, the daughter of Agni gave birth to six sons of great luster:
Aṅga, Sumanas, Svāti, Kratu, Aṅgiras, and Gaya.
From Aṅga, through the daughter of Sunītha, one son named Veṇa was born;
when Veṇa’s hand was churned, King Pṛthu came into being.
Then Pṛthu, the son of Vena and the first-born of the Kṣatriyas, protected this earth;
he was the lord of the earth and the first among those consecrated by the Rājasūya sacrifice.
From him were born two skillful sons, Suta and Māgadha;
moreover, two sons of Pṛthu, Antardhi and Pālina, were born who were knowers of dharma.
From Antardhāman was born Śikhaṇḍinī and Havirdhāna.
From the Havirdhāna shed, Dhīṣaṇā, who belongs to Agni, gave birth to the six Soma-pressings.
Prācīnavarhis, Śukra, Gaya, Kṛṣṇa, Vraja, and Ajina;
the venerable Prācīnavarhis was a great Prajāpati.
The lord took a wife from the daughter of the ocean;
Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis, beginning with Suvarṇa.
All of them were named Pracetas, masters of the science of archery;
having attained the status of Prajāpatis, they were satisfied with Prācīnavarhis.
The earth was indeed covered with trees, yet they burned those very trees. Then, perceiving the destruction of the forest while only a few trees remained,
King Soma, the Lord of Creatures, approached them and spoke to those Prajāpatis.
"Restrain your anger; they will give you their excellent daughter Māriṣā, born of the ascetic sage Kaṇḍu and of my own daughter Pramlocā."
Knowing the future, he created her for you as a wife who would perpetuate your lineage;
Dakṣa shall be born of her and will cause all creatures to multiply.
The Pracetasas accepted her, and from her Dakṣa was born;
then, from the ten Pracetasas and Māriṣā, the Prajāpati [Dakṣa] arose.
The highly effulgent Dakṣa was born from a portion of Soma; as a protector of the earth, he begot sons by the hundreds and thousands.
Indeed, five thousand sons of Dakṣa named Haryaśvas went out in all directions to ascertain the dimensions of the earth.
Then another thousand sons went out in search of them;
even today they have not returned, like rivers flowing into the oceans.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Lineage of Svāyambhuva," in the Vallālacarita of the Vyāsa Purāṇa.
Chapter Eleven. Siṃhagiri said:
From the mind of Brahmā came Atri, and Soma attained the status of his son;
I shall proclaim his lineage, O King, in which you were born.
Vyāsa said: Having performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, Soma gave the three worlds as the sacrificial fee to the principal members of the assembly, O subduers of enemies, those foremost Brahman-sages.
When the final purificatory bath was completed, the nine goddesses, their limbs tormented by the arrows of love and longing to behold his form, attended upon Soma.
Śinīvālī abandoned Kardama, Kratu himself abandoned Haviṣmat,
Dyuti abandoned Vibhāvasu, and Puṣṭi abandoned the imperishable Dhātṛ.
Then Prabhā abandoned Prabhākara, Vasu abandoned Mārīcikāśyapa, Kīrti abandoned her husband Jayanta, Dhṛti abandoned her husband Nandin,
and Lakṣmī abandoned Nārāyaṇa and devoted herself solely to Soma.
Then Soma also desired those illustrious women as if they were his own;
he indeed coveted Tārā by name, the glorious wife of Bṛhaspati.
Soma indeed swiftly carried off the pressed juice of the Aṅgirases;
though he was entreated by the gods together with the celestial rishis, Soma remained [unyielding].
At that time, he did not at all release Tārā to that descendant of Aṅgiras;
thereupon, Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, became enraged toward him.
Then Uśanas, the descendant of Aṅgiras, took up his rear guard;
for he was the highly resplendent disciple of his father, who had previously been the disciple of Bṛhaspati.
Out of that affection for Bṛhaspati, the Lord Rudra took up his bow, Āyagava, and became the protector of his rear.
By that high-souled one, the supreme weapon named Brahmaśiras was discharged against the Daityas, by which their fame was destroyed. There,
a terrible battle took place, renowned as the Tārakāmaya war.
It was a great conflict between the gods and the dānavas that brought about the destruction of the world.
Thereupon, those remaining gods, as well as the Tuṣitas and the earthly kings,
went for refuge to Brahmā, the primordial and eternal deity.
Brahmā, having restrained Uśanas, gave Tārā to Aṅgiras;
seeing that she was pregnant, the Guru said, "Abandon the fetus."
Then, cast from the womb while blazing, he said, "I am born of Soma.
Thus Budha was the son of Soma, and Purūravas was his son.
From that great-souled one, seven sons were born to Urvashi—a Gandharvi—and they were all of noble spirit: Āyu, Dhīmat, and Amāvasu.
Viśvāyu, the righteous Dharmātmā, and likewise Śrutāyu,
Dṛḍhāyu, Vanāyu, and Śatāyu were the sons of Urvaśī.
In ancient times, they were born of Prabhā, the daughter of Svarbhānu.
Siṃhagiri said:
"O Vallāla, in their lineages there were high-souled men of great prowess."
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras were born by the thousands.
Vyāsa said:
Āyus’s son was Nahuṣa; after him came Vṛddhaśarman, Rambha, Raji, and Anenas. Raji indeed had a hundred sons.
Raji, who had received boons from Viṣṇu, was renowned as "This is the King" (rājeyam);
at the request of the gods, he slew the Daityas in the war between the gods and the Asuras.
Seven sons of great power were born to Nahuṣa by Virajā, the daughter of Pitṛ; six of them possessed splendor equal to that of Indra.
Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Rāyāti, Pāñcika,
Bhava, and Suyāti as the sixth— among them, Yayāti indeed became the king of the earth.
The ascetic Yati, having attained liberation, became a sage who had become one with Brahman.
Of those five sons, Yayāti, having conquered this earth,
obtained Devayānī, the daughter of Uśanas, as his wife.
Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu, and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan and of Asura lineage, gave birth to Druhyu, Anu,
and Puru.
Yadu and Puru became the increasers of their respective lineages;
now hear of the lineage of that Yadu, which was endowed with marvelous prowess.
Yadu had five sons who were like the children of gods:
Sahasrada, Payoda, Kroṣṭā, Nīla, and Añjika.
The three heirs of Sahasrada were supremely righteous:
Haihaya, Haya, and King Veṇuhaya.
The wife of Haihaya was known as Dharmmanetra;
Dharmmanetra’s son was Kārta, and his son was Sāhañja. A city named Sāhañjanī was founded by that king.
The heir of Sāhañja was the king named Māhiṣmān;
by that monarch, the city named Māhīṣmatī was founded.
In ancient times, there was a powerful king named Bhadraśreṇya, the son of Mahiṣmat,
who was celebrated in the Purāṇas as the sovereign of Vārāṇasī.
The heir of Bhadraśreṇya was the renowned Durdamo;
the son of Durdamo was the king known as Kaṇaka.
From Kaṇaka were born Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtāgni, Karavīraka, and Kṛtaujas as the fourth; and from Kṛtavīrya came Arjuna.
He who, with his thousand arms, became the lord of the seven continents,
alone conquered the earth on a chariot as radiant as the sun.
Having forcibly deluded Rāvaṇa, the lord of Laṅkā, along with his army,
he bound him with the bowstrings and pierced him with five arrows.
Having utterly defeated him and brought him to Māhiṣmatī, he bound him;
for as he fought, a thousand arms appeared through the illusory power (*māyā*) of that Lord of Yoga, by virtue of his mastery over yoga.
"Oh, how great was the heroism of Bhārgava in battle,
when he lopped off the king's thousand arms like a grove of golden *tāla* trees!"—
thus [the people spoke] of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, as he was slaying the Kṣatriyas born of the arms [of royalty].
The queen of Kārtavīrya fled from that most terrible [encounter].
But that queen, while pregnant, gave birth in the hermitage of Kauśika to a son named Subhoma, as beautiful as the rising sun.
In due time, that lotus-faced son was reared by his mother;
the mighty-armed one received the science of archery from Kauśika.
Having heard that a Brahmin had killed his father,
the youth, his eyes red with rage, set out from his mother’s presence to slay the Brahmins in all directions.
Twenty-one times he made this earth devoid of Brāhmaṇas;
therefore, in the Kali age, Brāhmaṇas born from the mouth [of Brahmā] do not exist.
Then, having observed the Śavaras and the Kaḍhuka fishermen in that non-Brahminical region, Bhārgava composed for them the Sūtra.
Women are pleased by ornaments, cows by wandering at their own will, and elephants by a shower of dust; but what do these have to do with the reviling of others?
Then, in battle, the son of Arjuna struck down the son of Jamadagni;
thus, having conquered the Brahmins, that formidable Jayadhvaja became [renowned].
Then the Brahmins, desiring sons, approached the Kṣatriyas;
from them were born various lineages, such as the Kadamba-pallavas and others.
Tainted by the sin of killing a Brahmin, that king found no peace;
he performed the horse sacrifice (vājimedha), a rite that destroys all evil.
The stone images of those two still exist today in the beautiful city of Māhiṣmatī, on the bank of the river Narmadā.
Kārtavīrya had one hundred sons, of whom five were indeed preeminent:
Śūrasena, Śūra, Dhṛṣṭokta, Kṛṣṇa,
and the one known as Jayadhvaja, along with the mighty Subhoma.
From Jayadhvaja was born Tālajaṅgha; from Tālajaṅgha were born a hundred sons known as the Tālajaṅghas, who were heroes of supreme prowess.
In the exceedingly pure lineage of those high-souled Haihayas, the Vītihotras were born by themselves; they are known as the Bhojas and the Āvantyas.
The Taunḍikēyas are renowned, as are the Tālajaṅghas;
the Bharatas and the Sujātas have also been mentioned by me in the Purāṇa.
The heroic Yādavas, beginning with Vṛṣa, were performers of meritorious deeds;
among them, Vṛṣa was the sustainer of the lineage, and his son was Madhu.
Madhu had a hundred sons, but Vṛṣaṇa was the one who established his lineage;
from Vṛṣaṇa all were called Vṛṣṇis, while from Madhu they are known as the Mādhavas.

The Yādavas were born from Yadu, but they are not enumerated here due to their great number. From Turvaśa the Yavanas were born; the Bhojas are known as the sons of Druhyu; from Anu came the Mleccha tribes; and from Pūru, the Pauravas are recorded to have descended.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Lunar Lineage," in the *Vallālacarita* from the *Vyāsapurāṇa*.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Siṃhagiri said:

Listen, O King, to the lineage proclaimed by Vyāsa, characterized by supreme prowess, which has been told in detail and in its proper sequence— the lineage in which you yourself were born, O ruler of the earth.
Vyāsa said: Puru’s son was the immensely powerful King Janamejaya;
his son was Pracinvan, who conquered the eastern quarter.
From Pracinvat was born Pravīra, and his son was Manasyu;
the son of Manasyu was the king named Abhayada.
In the same way, the son of Abhayada was the king named Sudhanvan;
Sudhanvan’s son was Vahugava, and Sampāti was his son.
Sampāti was the son of Rahūgaṇa, and Raudrāśva was his son;
indeed, Raudrāśva had ten sons by the Apsaras Ghṛtācī.
Ṛceyu was the first among them; Kṛkaneyu was the second;
then Kakṣeyu, Sthaṇḍileyu, and the high-minded Sannateyu.
Daśārṇeya, Jaleyu, the mighty Sthaleyu,
Balanīya, and Baleyu— these were the ten sons of Rudrāśva.
From Kakṣeyu there were born three sons of great strength:
Sabhānara, Cākṣuṣa, and likewise Paramanthu.
The son of Sabhānara was the learned King Kālānala;
the son of Kālānala was indeed Sṛñjaya, who was a knower of dharma.
Sṛñjaya had a son, the heroic King Purañjaya;
the son of Purañjaya was the illustrious King Janamejaya.
The royal sage Mahāśāla was the son born of Janamejaya;
he was renowned among the gods and established his fame upon the earth.
A son named Mahāmanas was born to Mahāśāla; he was righteous, a hero honored by hosts of warriors, and truly great-minded.
That most excellent man, Mahāmanas, begot two sons:
Uśīnara, who was knower of dharma, and Titikṣu, who possessed great strength.
The wives of Uśīnara were born from the lineages of five royal seers:
Mṛgā, Kṛmi, Navā, Darvā, and the fifth was Dṛṣadvatī.
The five sons of Uśīnara, who perpetuated his lineage,
were born through great asceticism as the offspring of that aged man.
To Nṛgā was born a son, Nṛga; from Kṛmi was born Kṛmi;
to Navā was born a son, Nava; and from Darvā, Suvrata was born.
From Dṛṣadvatī was born King Śivi Auśīnara;
from Śibi came the famous Śivis, and from Mṛga the Yaudheyas.
From Nava came Navarāṣṭra, and from Kṛmi the city of Kṛmilā.
Likewise, the Ambaṣṭhas are the sons of Suvrata; learn now of the sons of Śibi.
Śiva, however, had four sons, world-renowned,
namely Vṛṣadarbha, Suvīra, Kaikeya, and Madraka.
Their prosperous territories were Kaikeya and Madra, as well as Vṛṣadarbha and Suvīra; now hear of the offspring of Titikṣu.
O King, the kings in the eastern direction were the Taitikṣus;
Uṣadratha was a great being, and Phena was his son.
From Phena was born Sutapā; from Sutapā was born Bali.
Having been born into human lineage, he became the king Kāñcaneṣudhi.
In ancient times, that great yogi became King Bali;
he begot five sons who established lineages upon the earth.
First Aṅga was born, then Vaṅga and Suhma;
likewise Puṇḍra and Kaliṅga—these are called the Bāleya Kṣatriyas.
The Bāleyas and the Brāhmaṇas were the founders of his lineage on earth;
for Bali, the wise and pleased Brahmā granted this boon: ||| 25 ||
The state of being a great yogi, a lifespan measured by the duration of a kalpa, invincibility in battle, preeminence in dharma,
the vision of the three worlds, and likewise preeminence in procreation.
O Bala, you shall indeed possess incomparable power and the vision of the true nature of reality;
you shall establish the four castes in their fixed positions.
When this was said by the Lord, King Bali attained supreme peace.
Having consecrated those five sinless sons here,
that lord, having accomplished his purpose and with his self united in yoga, took recourse to yoga.
Invincible to all beings, the sage wanders about awaiting his time.
After a long time, the steadfast one returned to his own abode;
their five provinces were Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Suhma.
The Kaliṅgas and the Puṇḍrakas were the subjects of Aṅga; listen now to [the lineage of] Aṅga’s son: there was a great lord of kings named Dadhivāhana.
The son of Dadhivāhana was King Diviratha;
his son was the learned Dharmaratha, and Citraratha was his son.
Then, on Mount Viṣṇupada, while performing a sacrifice together with Śakra upon that chariot of Dharma, the high-souled one drank the Soma.
Now, Citraratha also had a son named Daśaratha, who was known as Lomapāda; his daughter was Śāntā.
By the grace of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, a heroic son of Daśaratha was born to him— highly renowned, possessed of the fourfold army, and the increaser of his lineage.
The son of Caturaṅga was known as Pṛthulākṣa;
the son of Pṛthulākṣa was the highly illustrious king named Campa.
The city of Campa was formerly known as Mālinī;
by the grace of Pūrṇabhadra, Haryyakṣa became his son.
Then Vaibhāṇḍaki, by means of mantras, brought down to earth that supreme mount, the elephant who wards off enemies. The heir of Haryyakṣa is known as King Bhadraratha.
The son of Bhadraratha was Vṛhatkarman, a lord of subjects.
His son was Vṛhadarbha, from whom [came] Vṛhanmanas at the sacrifice;
and Vṛhanmanas, the lord of kings, begot a son.
From him was born the hero Jayadratha by name;
from Dṛḍharatha came King Dṛḍharatha, and the joy of his lineage was Viśvajit.
Karna was his heir, and Vikarṇa was his son;
he had a hundred sons who increased the lineage of the Aṅgas.
The son of Vṛhadarbha was the king named Vṛhanmanas;
he had two wives, both auspicious daughters of Vinatā.
There were Yaśodevī and Satyā; from them the lineage arose.
Jayadratha, the lord of kings, was born of Yaśodevī.
Satyā’s son was named Vijaya, who is remembered as one who excelled among the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas; Vijaya’s son was Dhṛti, and his son was Dhṛtavrata.
The son of Dhṛtavrata was the highly illustrious Satyakarman;
his son was Adhiratha, who was also known by the other name Sūta.
He who adopted Karṇa was the one by whom Karṇa, the son of a Sūta, was raised;
Vṛṣasena was the son of Karṇa, and Pṛthusena was his son.
In the lineage of Pṛthusena, there will be a hero named Vīrasena,
who shall marry Somaṭā, the daughter of a Gauḍa Brahmin.
Born into that lineage, heroic kings of immeasurable prowess will bring the lords of the seven continents under their command.
In his lineage, having become Sāmantasena, he will be a powerful protector of the earth,
which is bounded by the Vindhya mountains on one side and the bridge of Setubandha on the other, and clothed by the ocean.
Siṃhagiri said:
"Therefore, O King, Hemantasena was your grandfather;
he was the abode of splendors and greatness, and a fire to the armies of his enemies."
From him was born King Vijayasena, a friend of Cōḍagaṅga,
who conquered the entire earth girdled by the four oceans.
You are the son of that Vallāla Sārvabhauma, the lord of the earth,
to whom the rival rulers of the world have come for refuge.
The lineage of the Senas, born from that [lineage] which is the source of the Brahman and Kṣatriya castes and the first-born of the Kṣatriyas— even though you were born into it, O Pāṇḍava.
The fool who hates the Pāṇḍava and the evil-minded one who reviles him shall become a worm in excrement and be cooked in hell for a long time.
That moon which is the beloved of ten thousand moons, the moon that is the delight of his loved ones—
O Great King, it is now time for him to carry out his royal decree.
He has a jewel of a daughter whose beauty is peerless on earth;
like Nābhāga taking Suprabhā, O Paurava, carry off that maiden. Whenever that young girl goes to the Uccandra lake to bathe, she appears as a radiant fair-complexioned woman.
Then, at that very moment, the dawn-red sun hastens her to behold him who is even redder than itself.
When two watches of the night remain and they perceive the dawn of the sun,
merchants do not trust in their debtors.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Genealogy of the Pūru Lineage," in the Vallālacarita from the Vyāsa Purāṇa.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—desire born of right resolve: this is remembered as the root of Dharma.
Teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts— these are declared to be the duties of Brāhmaṇas.
The Śruti and Smṛti are the two eyes of the Brahmins, ordained by the gods;
one who is deprived of one of them is called one-eyed, while one who lacks both is proclaimed to be blind.
A householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rules in the nuptial fire,
as well as the performance of the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking of food.

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation of water is the sacrifice to the ancestors; the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali offering is the sacrifice to the beings; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men.
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— though he breathes, he does not truly live.
A Brahmin staying for a single night is considered a guest (*atithi*), as is a Kṣatriya;
for since his stay is uncertain, he is therefore called a guest.
Even if a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at his household as a guest,
he should feed them along with his servants, demonstrating compassion.
He should always be devoted to his own wife and avoid the wives of others.
Having performed the fire-oblation, the noble-minded one should eat in the evening and in the morning.
A twice-born man who is distressed by a lack of livelihood may accept gifts from anyone;
he incurs no fault thereby, for he is equal to fire and the sun.
The protection of living beings, giving, sacrifice, study,
the worship of Śiva, and likewise the worship of Nārāyaṇa— these are the duties of Kṣatriyas.
Constantly exerting himself in the destruction of bandits in battle, he should display his prowess;
for there is no task more important for a king than the suppression of bandits.
He should protect the subjects from flatterers, bards, thieves, and those who commit great acts of violence, and especially from the scribes.
A Kṣatriya should always cause the Vaidikas to dwell [among him] with honors, gifts, and respectful treatment;
and he should indeed perform his religious duties with great effort.
One should always protect a wise person who knows the treatises on ethics;
joined by the virtuous, one should always appoint such a person in the midst of the assembly.
One should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments and likewise awaken to that same sound;
one should contemplate the scriptures with the intellect, as well as all that ought to be done.
Having seen [these omens], he should give cows, gold, and land to those who know the stars and to physicians,
as well as dwellings and houses for those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).
Whatever dharma belongs to a king in the protection of his own kingdom,
that very same dharma he attains in its entirety when bringing another's kingdom under his control.
Devoted to the gods and the brahmins, intent upon the rites for the ancestors,
and always devoted to his own wife, the king is always worthy of receiving a sixth part [of the produce].
One part of the force should be maintained [in reserve], two parts for gifts,
one part for the subjects, and one part for the officials.
With one part for his own enjoyment and for the maintenance of his family and so forth,
the lord of the earth should thus make his expenditures from the income divided into six portions.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he engages in captivating song and instrumental music,
or in dancing, singing, and eating at night with women, which brings him pleasure.
A Vaiśya should duly engage in the protection of cattle, agriculture, and trade;
he should give gifts according to his ability and provide food for the Brāhmaṇas.
Free from hypocrisy and delusion, likewise free from speech and envy,
devoted to his own wife, self-controlled, and avoiding the wives of others.

Having fed the Brahmins with wealth at the time of sacrifice, as well as the officiating priests, he should live without personal ownership over wealth until the fall of his body, remaining steadfast in his duties.

One should constantly perform sacrifices, Vedic study, and acts of charity without indolence; one should likewise be devoted to the rites for the ancestors and intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu and Śiva.
A Śūdra should diligently perform service for the three castes; he should especially conduct himself toward Brāhmaṇas as if he were their slave.
He should be one who gives without being asked; he may resort to agriculture for his livelihood, as well as the pure occupations of an artisan or a wandering performer.
One should worship the gods tirelessly according to the rules for the *pākayajña* sacrifices;
however, service to the twice-born is proclaimed as his supreme duty.
Wearing worn-out clothes, eating the remnants of a Brahmin's meal,
taking pleasure in one's own wife, and avoiding the wives of others;
salt, honey, oil, curd, buttermilk, ghee, and milk.
One should not find fault with those of the Śūdra caste; one may perform the sale of all [goods].
For all [castes], a blameless livelihood through wages is obtained by various occupations;
agriculture with various types of ploughs is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas and the others by Manu and other authorities.
Having seen a plough drawn by sixteen oxen for Brahmins, by four fewer than that for others, by two oxen for those of the lowest castes, or even one ox for those who live on the land; Valc_2,13.33.
Having broken the earth, having cut down plants, and having killed insects and ants,
farmers indeed purify themselves through sacrifice and the worship of the gods.

For the twice-born, the purifying refinement of the body— beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception rite) and performed through meritorious Vedic rituals— should be carried out, as it leads to sanctification both in this world and after death.
The *garbhādhāna* rite is performed during the fertile period; the *pumsavana* before the fetus moves; the *sīmantonnayana* in the fourth or eighth month; and upon birth, the *jātakarman*.
The departure [from the womb] occurs in the third month; the naming ceremony takes place when a hundred days have dawned;
the first feeding of solid food occurs in the sixth month; and the tonsure ceremony occurs in the year of birth or according to family custom.

The piercing of the ears, the instruction in vows, the commencement of Vedic study, the ritual procedures, the tonsure ceremony, the ceremonial bath, marriage, and the formal adoption of the nuptial fire; Valc_2,13.38 //
And the maintenance of the three sacred fires—these are recorded as the sixteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*).
These nine, ending with the piercing of the ears, are performed for a woman without mantras.
A Brahmin is eligible for the initiation ceremony (*vratopanaya*) in the eighth year from conception, a Kṣatriya likewise in the eleventh,
and one born of the Vaiśya caste in the twelfth.
For one who has undertaken a vow, this time [for its completion] may be twice as long or more;
however, one who has fallen from the Vedic vows is a *vrātya*, and such a *vrātya* deserves the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Āsura; the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest.
These four dharmas were previously proclaimed for the Brahmin;
however, the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa are praised for the Kṣatriya.
The *brāhma* marriage is proclaimed as that which is performed without solicitation or effort;
the *prājāpatya* is proclaimed as that which is performed by granting the requested bride-price.
The Āsura [form] arises from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, from mutual agreement;
the Rākṣasa, from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca, from the deception of the maiden.
Three wives are prescribed for a Kṣatriya, one wife for a Brāhmaṇa,
and only one wife is ordained for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra.
A Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, and a Śūdra woman are proclaimed as wives for a Kṣatriya; however, for a Brāhmaṇa, only one wife is ordained, and that is a Brāhmaṇa woman.
A Vaiśya woman is declared to be the wife of a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra woman that of a Śūdra;
a Brāhmaṇa should never marry a maiden of a different caste.
The Ambaṣṭha who was born from a Vaiśya woman by a Brāhmaṇa has indeed attained the status of a Śūdra; therefore, he may not marry from among the Vaiśyas.
That which is declared regarding the loss of caste for a Kṣatriya who has a Śūdra wife should not be understood as my own opinion, because she is elevated by him through that very act.
A Brahmin and a Vaiśya fall from their caste by marrying a Śūdra girl;
however, there is no loss of caste for a Kṣatriya from taking a Śūdra woman as his wife.
In ancient times, marriages with the daughters of Brahmins were also performed by royal sages;
for those possessed of great luster, this is not a fault, just as fire is not a fault when it consumes everything.
Manu said: "Our king must not be disregarded as if he were a mere mortal."
For this is a great deity who dwells in human form.
That which has been performed by the gods and that which has been performed by the sages should not be performed by humans; rather, one should perform the action as it has been prescribed.
When a woman of his own caste has been married, a non-Brahmin may indeed marry as he desires;
a son begotten upon her does not fall from the status of one born of a wife of equal caste.
One born from a Kṣatriya man and a Kṣatriya woman shall be a Kṣatriya, without a doubt;
and likewise, one born from a Vaiśya woman, or even from a Śūdra woman, shall be the same.
As long as a man does not find a wife, he remains only half;
for nothing is produced as a whole until it is born, so says the Śruti.
If a maiden approaches him with desire, there is no transgression in their union;
however, having adorned and honored her, he alone shall marry her.

For the sake of accomplishing dharma, a king should first marry a wife of his own caste; thereafter, he may marry according to his desire, following the order of castes without descending to a lower one.
Just as nectar is to be taken from poison, gold from filth,
and supreme knowledge from a low person, so too is a jewel of a woman to be taken from a base family.
Women, jewels, as well as knowledge, dharma, purity, eloquent speech,
and various arts— these are to be accepted from everywhere.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all ritual actions there become fruitless.
For the sake of procreation, these highly fortunate women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
between women and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) in households, there is no distinction whatsoever.
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those already born, and the daily conduct of worldly life—women are visibly the foundation for all this. (Valc 2,13.64)
Offspring, the duties of marriage, service, and supreme delight—all these depend upon the wife; likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself indeed depends upon her.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Duties of the Castes and Other Matters," in the *Vallālacarita* from the *Vyāsapurāṇa*.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
A woman praised [as a consort] is one whose every limb is beautiful, who walks with the gait of an elephant in rut,
whose thighs and hips are full, and whose eyes are like those of the black antelope.
Her hair was dark, her limbs slender, and her body hair fine; she was enchanting.
Her feet touched the ground evenly, and likewise her breasts were well-knit together.
The navel is clockwise-rotating; the private parts are like those of the *aśvattha* tree;
the ankles are well-concealed; the navel is the size of a thumb;
the cheeks resemble the flowers of the *madhūka* tree; and [the limbs] are neither veiny nor hairy.
She does not knit her brows in frowns; she is the very life of her husband and is dear to him.
In her childhood, she rejoices in playthings and the eating of divine fruits provided at the proper times;
as a young woman, she delights in garments, ornaments, embraces, and the like.
A woman of middle age should take delight through her skill in the arts of love-play;
an elderly woman, however, should be joined with sweet conversation and dignity.
At sixteen years she is a girl; at thirty, she possesses youthful vigor;
at fifty-five, she is mature; and beyond that, she is an old woman.
Women are indeed dependent on desire; for that purpose, there is the collection of jewels.
A king who seeks sensual pleasures should enjoy them, yet not indulge excessively.
When a woman is sixteen years old, a man of twenty-four years—
A wise person should exert effort out of a desire for distinguished happiness.
Thus, those two, possessing the full vigor of their limbs, procreate a supreme son,
endowed with all his faculties, powerful, and destined for a hundred-year lifespan.
A young woman is considered beneficial for those with sensual desires during the summer and autumn; she is weak then.
In the cold season, a middle-aged woman is beneficial; likewise, a middle-aged woman is recommended during the rainy season and spring.
A young woman, when constantly cultivated, always increases one's strength;
a young woman diminishes one's vitality, while a middle-aged woman brings on old age.
Fresh meat, śāli rice, the company of young women, ghee,
milk, and bathing in warm water— these six are the immediate restorers of life.
A man of desire who has been strengthened by aphrodisiacs may indulge according to his wish even in the cold season;
however, he should indulge in sexual union to his heart's content at the onset of the cool season.
In the cold season at night, during the day in summer, both by day and night in spring,
in the rainy season with the roar of clouds, and in autumn— he was full of longing.
Desirous and having first excited her with embraces and other such acts,
he— strengthened by aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa)— should approach the woman with skillful means.
Bathing daily in warm water, drinking milk, young women,
kings— this is your wholesome regimen, provided with plenty of unctuous substances and moderate food.
By means of a mixture of *kapittha* powder, as well as with curd and earth, the ghee becomes fragrant; likewise, by throwing milk and barley [into it].
Such is the preparation of food; now the release of fragrance is demonstrated.
Proper purification, ritual sipping of water, and likewise the act of purging.
Cultivation, ripening, awakening, fumigation, and likewise perfuming—
this is declared to be the eightfold ritual action as it is traditionally remembered.
Having prepared water with the tender leaves of the *kapittha*, *bilva*, *jambu*, *āmra*, and *karavīraka* trees,
whatever substance is purified by it is indeed cleansed.
In their absence, purification may be achieved with the water of musk-deer musk;
[the substances are] nakha, kuṣṭha, ghana, māṃsa, spṛkkā, and water from śaileya.
Likewise, saffron, lac, sandalwood, agallochum, nīrada,
sarala, and devakāṣṭha, along with a skull-bowl and a beloved woman.
Bāla, kunduraka, guggulu, and śrīnivāsaka,
together with sarjarasa, constitute the twenty-one incense substances.
From this group of twenty-one incense substances, one should take two substances at a time according to one's desire and combine them with portions of *sarja* resin.
By combining these with lac, sesame seeds, and lotuses, along with honey,
incense preparations are formed here according to one's own desire, as prescribed.
Bark, tubers, fruit, oil, saffron, granthiparṇaka,
śaileya, tagara, kāntā, and camphor from the Chola country.
One should prescribe māṣī, murā, and kuṣṭha as the substances for bathing. Having taken these three substances according to one's desire,
along with musk, a bath should be performed that increases passion.
A bath with equal parts of tvak, murā, and analada, combined with half as much vāsa, will have the fragrance of blue lotus; when mixed with oil, it takes on the scent of saffron.
It shall be as fragrant as jasmine flowers when combined with half a portion of tagara;
it shall be a fine perfume, enchanting and equal in scent to vakula blossoms.
Having added mañjiṣṭhā, tagara, cola, tvac, vyāghranakha, nakha,
and gandhapatra, there will be auspicious fragrant oil.
Oil from sesame seeds becomes fragrant with jasmine and is dear to women;
when oil is pressed from sesame seeds that have been scented with flowers,
it will certainly become identical to the flower in fragrance through that perfuming.
Cardamom, cloves, kakkola, nutmeg, and camphor,
together with cinnamon leaves, are independent mouth-fresheners.
Camphor, saffron, *kāntā*, musk, *hareṇuka*,
*kakkola*, cardamom, cloves, jasmine, and *kośaka*.
Cinnamon bark, cardamom, musta, the latā, as well as musk,
the thorns of the clove tree, and the fruit and leaves of the jāti flower.
Having taken *kuṭaja* fruit, one should prepare it in the measure of a *karṣa*;
to that powder, one should add the heartwood of *khadira* in a fourth part, having first infused it.
From this [powder], auspicious pills should be made with the juice of *sahakāra* (mango).
Placed in the mouth, these fragrant pills destroy diseases of the mouth. // Valc 2.14.37 //
Betel nut that has been thoroughly washed with water from the five sprouts,
along with pills and substances according to one's ability, serves as an aromatic for the mouth.
The tooth-stick should be pungent and infused with cow’s urine for three days.
And it was properly prepared like betel, serving as a fragrance for the mouth.
When equal portions of cinnamon and cardamom are combined with half a portion of camphor,
it shines like betel leaf as a captivating mouth-freshener.
Thus should the lord of the earth always protect women;
yet he should never place his trust in them, especially not in their sons or mothers.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of Women," in the Vallālacarita from the Vyāsapurāṇa.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is paramount; and in the Kali age, charity is the only way.
There exists no higher duty for living beings in this world than the duty of giving;
it should be bestowed by one desiring heaven, long life, prosperity, and for the sake of the pacification of evil.
Nothing is seen in the three worlds that is superior to giving;
by giving one attains heaven, and through giving alone is prosperity obtained.
Through giving one conquers enemies; through giving, disease is destroyed;
through giving, knowledge is obtained; and through giving, one gains the company of young women.
Through giving one obtains enjoyments, and through giving one finds long life;
it is remembered as the supreme means for achieving virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
One should give a gift facing east, and one should receive it facing north;
thus the lifespan of the giver increases, and that of the receiver does not diminish.
A gift to a mother is said to be a hundredfold; a gift to a father is a thousandfold;
a gift to a daughter is infinite; and what is given to a uterine sister is inexhaustible.
A gift given to a non-human being is known to have great fruit when given to a sinner;
a gift to one of mixed caste yields double that, and to a Śūdra, fourfold.
To a Vaiśya it is eightfold, and to a Kṣatriya, sixteenfold; to one who merely calls himself a twice-born, it is likewise sixteenfold.
The merit is a hundredfold for one who studies the Vedas, and infinite for one who imparts the understanding of the Vedas.
A gift given to a guru, a domestic priest, and the like is said to be inexhaustible;
that which is given to those devoid of prosperity, as well as to one who performs sacrifices, is infinite.
Fearlessness has all the gods as its deity; the earth indeed has Viṣṇu as its deity;
daughters, male slaves, and female slaves are proclaimed to have Prajāpati as their deity.
The elephant is said to belong to Prajāpati, and the horse has Yama as its deity.
Likewise, all single-hoofed animals belong to Yama, as does the buffalo.
The camel belongs to Nairṛta; the cow to Rudra; the goat and the sheep to Agni;
the ram to Āpa; and the monkey and the boar are the wild animals belonging to Niḷa.
A reservoir of water belongs to Varuṇa; water-vessels such as jars and the like belong to him as well.
Jewels born of the ocean, gold, iron, and fire likewise belong to him.
Grains belong to Prajāpati; kings say that cooked food belongs to the Earth;
fragrance is said to belong to Gandharva; and clothing is traditionally held to belong to Bṛhaspati.
All birds belong to Vāyu; likewise, the Brāhmī [Vidyā] and its ancillaries, as well as books and the like, belong to Sarasvatī; while Viśvakarman presides over the arts.
The trees and other such plants are the substance-deities (dravyadeva), the body of Hari;
likewise, the parasol, the black antelope skin, the bed, the chariot, and the seat are his very form.
Likewise, sandals, a vehicle, the eight [limbs], O Aṅgiras,
the equipment for a chariot, weapons, banners, and so forth— all these have the deities as their presiding deities.
The house has all deities as its presiding deities, and for everyone, Viṣṇu is the deity;
or else Śiva, because there is indeed no substance whatsoever that exists apart from them.
Listen, I shall proclaim the sixteen great gifts (mahādānas).
First is the tulāpuruṣa, then the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha,
the Brahmāṇḍa, the Kalpavṛkṣa, and the thousand cows as the fifth.
The Golden Wish-Cow, and the Golden Horse as the seventh;
likewise the Golden Horse-Chariot, and similarly the Golden Elephant-Chariot.
Likewise, the gift of land consisting of five ploughs yields great fruit;
the twelfth is the Viṣṇucakra, and after that, the Kalpalatā.
On an auspicious day, one should offer the gift of the seven oceans, as well as the jewel-cow, and likewise the vessel of the great elements.
In the pavilion, within the mandala, one should offer the gift to the gods; one should address the Brahmin as "O god" and say, "I give," while uttering the name of the substance.
Then one should offer water into the hand; this is remembered as the rule for giving. Having mentally designated the recipient, one should pour water upon the ground.
The end of the ocean exists, but the end of giving does not exist.
To one who possesses a name, belongs to a specific lineage, and has such-and-such ancestors;
who is endowed with the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; who is a worthy recipient and a truly great soul.
For the increase of the merit and fame of one's mother, father, and oneself;
for the pacification of all misdeeds; for the sake of heaven, and for the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"Just as this great object, named [so-and-so], has Viṣṇu, Rudra, and other deities as its presiding divinities, so I bestow it upon you; may Hari and Śiva be pleased with me."
"For the sake of establishing this gift, I give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
With this formula for giving, one should indeed offer all gifts.
When gold is being given, however, silver is prescribed as the sacrificial fee.
For other types of gifts as well, gold is traditionally prescribed as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Gold, silver, copper, rice, and grain as well—
this daily ancestral rite (*nityaśrāddha*) and the worship of the gods (*devapūjā*) are all performed without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*).
Silver is the sacrificial fee for rites pertaining to the ancestors; it is the means for accomplishing dharma, desire, and wealth.
Gold, silver, copper, gems, pearls, and riches [are likewise appropriate].
O woman of great wisdom, one who gives land bestows all of this:
the ancestors residing in the world of the fathers, and the deities in the realm of the gods.
The one of peaceful mind who gives away the earth—
whether it be a small town, a hamlet, or even a village rich in grain— satisfies [the ancestors].
By giving land measuring even a hundred nivartanas, or half of that,
or even just enough for sowing and reaping, one becomes a partaker of its fruit.
He who gives land covered with sugarcane, barley, wheat,
and rice to one learned in the Vedas is not born again.
Having given land that has been ploughed, together with its trees and abounding in crops,
one is honored in heaven for as long as the light of the sun's rays endures.
And one should give to a Brahmin endowed with virtues, devoted to austerities, and having conquered his senses;
[the merit lasts] as long as the earth remains bounded by the oceans.
For that long, his fruit shall be infinite.
Just as seeds sown upon the surface of the earth sprout,
even so do desires grow when acquired through the gift of land.
Just as a drop of oil fallen upon water immediately spreads out,
so too a gift bestowed upon the ground grows when there is grain to be harvested.
O King, the giver of food is always happy, the giver of clothing is handsome,
and that man who gives the earth is a giver of everything.
Just as a milch cow, yielding milk, nourishes her calf by providing its milk,
even so does the earth, when bestowed, nourish the giver of land, O protector of the earth.
Āditya, Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Soma, Hutāśana,
and the Lord who wields the trident— all these rejoice in the giver of land.
The ancestors clap their hands and the grandfathers praise him, saying:
"A giver of land has been born into our lineage; he shall be our savior."
The earth has been given away by many kings, beginning with Sagara;
to whomever the land belongs at any time, to him alone belongs the fruit thereof.
He who accepts land and he who bestows land—
both of them are performers of meritorious deeds, destined for the heavenly realm.
The king should grant land or a fixed income, and having done so, he should cause a deed to be executed for the information of future benevolent rulers.
On a cloth or on a copper plate,
the lord of the earth should have inscribed his own lineage and himself, marked with his own seal.
Having described the boundaries of the gift and the limits of the land granted,
he should cause a firm edict to be issued, complete with his own hand and the date.
O kings, by bestowing gifts of gold, gifts of cows, and gifts of land,
one is liberated from all sins.
Gold is the first offspring of Agni.
The earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun;
he who gives gold, a cow,
and land has effectively given all three worlds.
He who constructs a new pond, or even has an old one excavated, uplifts his entire lineage and is glorified in the heavenly world. (Valc 2.15.54)
Even after committing sinful deeds, he who gives food to one who asks—
especially to a Brāhmaṇa— is not tainted by that sin.
Having delivered three times seven generations of his family, the giver of a maiden shall partake in the world of Brahmā;
and by constructing a temple and an image, one shall obtain everything.
By giving a female slave to the best of the twice-born, one shall attain the world of the Apsarases;
O kings, fire shall never burn his organ of generation.
Siṃhagiri said:

Having bestowed many female slaves— well-adorned with garments, ornaments, perfumes, and flowers, their bodies beautiful and desirable due to their youthful form— upon the most excellent of the twice-born, King Śrīlādiśūra rejoices as if with celestial nymphs.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Greatness of Giving," in the Vallālacarita from the Vyāsa Purāṇa.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
The preceptor, the father, the elder brother, and the sovereign;
the maternal uncle, the father-in-law, the protector, and the maternal and paternal grandfathers.
The eldest brother and the paternal uncle are remembered as elders among men;
likewise, the mother, the maternal grandmother, and the father’s and mother’s sisters, and so forth.

O kings, the mother-in-law, the paternal grandmother, the elder sister, and the nurse are women who are gurus; thus has this group of gurus been described, both from the side of the mother and the side of the father.
One should follow their will through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Upon seeing his teacher, he should rise and salute him with palms joined;
he should not sit down together with these [elders], nor should he dispute with them for his own sake.

One should never speak out of hatred toward one's teachers, even for the sake of saving one's life; for one who harbors hatred toward their teachers falls low, even if they are distinguished by other virtues.
Of all gurus, these five are to be honored with diligence;
among them, the first three are the most excellent, and among those, the mother is the most venerable.
He who imparts instruction, she who gives birth, he by whom one's knowledge is taught,
the elder brother, and the husband— these five are remembered as gurus.
One who desires prosperity should especially honor these five with every effort, even at the cost of one's own life.
There is no deity equal to a father; there is no teacher equal to a mother. (Valc 2.16.8)
One should always do what is pleasing to those two through action, mind, and speech;
