without being authorized by them, one should not resort to any other duty.
The teacher is the preceptor of the twice-born; among the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor;
the husband alone is the preceptor of women; and everywhere, the guest is a preceptor.
That best of men who bows to a brahmin with the thought that he is Viṣṇu,
his lifespan, sons, fame, and prosperity increase.
Even a twice-born man of immoral conduct is worthy of honor, but not a Śūdra who has conquered his senses;
for Brāhmaṇas possess the nature of Kṣatriyas and must never be treated with contempt.
The twice-born, mounted upon the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wielding the sword of the Vedas,
whatever they may declare— even in jest— that is remembered as the supreme Dharma.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Lineage of Gurus," in the Vallālacarita from the Vyāsapurāṇa.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Mānava, Kāśyapa, Kāṅkāyana, Rahūgaṇa, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Kalviṣa, and Sukālina; Valc 2.17.1.
Ārṣṭiṣeṇa and Agniveśa, Kṛṣṇa, Cyavana, and Vasiṣṭha; Viśvāmitra and Gālava, Candrātreya and Kauśika.
Ghṛtakauśika and Maudgalya, Lābhāyana and Parāśara, Saupāyana, Atri, and Kuhala, as well as Vāsuki and Rohita. Valc_2,17.3 //
Vārdhyaśva, Vaiyāghrapadya, Darbha, Śālāvata, Kapi,
Jamadagni, Kāñcana, Kātyāyana, and Vṛhaspati.
Viśuvṛddha Sāṅkṛtya, Garga, Kauṇḍinya and Baṃpula, Sāvarṇa Āṅgirasa, Mauna, Kauśya, Yaugana and Jaimini. Valc 2.17.5.
Śakti, Kātyāyana, Vātsya, Logākṣi, and likewise Śunaka;
Agasti, Somarāja, Sandāna, Mādhava, and Bhṛgu.
Maitrāyaṇi, Śāṇḍilya, Upamanyu, Dhanañjaya, Madhukulya, Hārita, Vidala, and likewise Gobhila.
Kāśakāyana and Yāska, Vārṣṇeya, Brahmakṣatraka, Yuvanāśva, Vaiṇya, Jātūkarṇa, Aghamarṣaṇa,
Ambarīṣa, Idhmavāha, Lauhitya, and Indrakauśika.
Aja, Nidhruva, Rebha, and the sages who were the founders of lineages.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of Lineages," in the *Vallālacarita* from the *Vyāsapurāṇa*.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
The royal sages said:
O one of great wisdom, tell us the distinctions among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and those of low birth; we have a supreme curiosity to hear it.
Vyāsa said:
The Sārasvatas, Kānyakubjas, Gauḍas, Maithilas, and Otkalas—
these are known as the five Gauḍas who dwell to the north of the Vindhya mountains.
The Karṇāṭas, Tailaṅgas, Gurjjaras, and the inhabitants of Rāṣṭra;
the Andhras and Drāviḍas—these five dwell to the south of the Vindhya mountains.
But first, the Brahmins emerged from the solar disc like blazing suns and descended upon Śākadvīpa.
Thus are the groups of Brahmins:
the Pāṇḍavas, Pauravas, Baudhas, Sahasrārjunas, Haihayas,
Candrātreyas, Kalacuris, Raṭṭas, Yādavas, and Tomaras.
The Kauśikas, Kaukurās, and Kuśyas are proclaimed as the Saumyas;
likewise the Aikṣvākus, Nikumbhas, Mauryas, and Sāgaras;
as well as the Kacchapaghātas, Rāghavas, and Gobhilas.
Likewise, the Gāhaḍavālas—these are proclaimed as the Sauras.
The Cāhamānas, the Mallas, the Chindas, the Apotkaṭas,
as well as the Caulūkyas, the Silāras, the Hūnas, and those born of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya castes.
Born from the sacrificial fire-pit, the supreme and mighty Śālukikas and Sendrakas are known as the Kādraveyas.
From Veṇa was born Pṛthu, the son of Vainya; from him arose those who seize the earth.
The Vainateyas and Tārkṣyas, however, were the lowest of Kṣatriyas, known as the Pālās.
Thus ends the section on the Kṣatriyas:
Upakeśāśva, Prākvāṭa, Rohita, and Mahotsava;
likewise, the disciples from Māhiṣmatī, Vaiśālī, and Kauśāmbī.
The merchants of Ayodhyā are renowned on earth, as are the wealthy Gurjaras;
the Ujānikas are affluent, while the Suvarṇas are the lowest of merchants.
The third group of merchants was born from the rays of the moon.
Thus ends the section on the Vaiśyas.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Section on the Three Castes," in the *Vyāsapurāṇa* concerning the life of Vallāla.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
There is both the *sat-śūdra* and the *śūdra*; indeed, the *śūdra* is considered to be of two kinds.
The first is born from a *śūdra* woman by a Brahmin or a Vaiśya; the second is recorded as being born from a *pāda* (foot).
From a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya maiden is born the one named Maula;
from a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya maiden, the son is known as an Ambaṣṭha.
From an Ambaṣṭha man and a Vaiśya woman is born one named Vaidya;
from a Vaiśya man and a Śūdra woman is born a Karaṇa; and from that same Karaṇa man and a Karaṇī woman, one is born who stands among the ranks of the Karaṇas and is therefore called a Kāyastha.
There are those born of the Pādas who reside as Kāyasthas, and likewise those born of the Ambaṣṭhas; however, those Kirātas who are Kāyasthas are all considered censurable.
Nigama and Gandhika, both born of the Vaiśya lineage,
gradually attained the status of Śūdras due to causes such as the neglect of sacred rites.
[They became] jewel-workers, goldsmiths, silver-workers, and scribes.
Coppersmiths, ironworkers, conch-shell workers, and lute-players;
Those born from a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother are proclaimed as Taṇḍulinas, and those from a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother as Vyañjaninas; these are the Sat-Śūdras.
From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother are born the Rāmakas and Vaidehas, who are the sons of a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya respectively.
From a Rāmaṇa and a Kṣatriya maiden is born one named Ugra;
from a Brāhmaṇa and an Ugra maiden is born one named Āvṛta.
From a Vaiśya and a Vaideha woman—who is the daughter of a Brātya Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya—a Śūdra Ābhīra is born;
from that same Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman, a Kāṃsakāra is born.
From a Vaiśya, two sons, Gopa and Gopālaka, were born of an Ambaṣṭha woman;
and from a Rāmaka, a Leṣakāra was born of a Vaidehaka woman.
From a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is born one known as a *tailakāra* (oil-maker). From a Svarṇakāra father and an Ambaṣṭhā mother is born one named a *śaucika* (cleaner).
From a Vaiśya and the daughter of a weaver, one named Kṛṣika is born;
from a Kṛṣika and the daughter of a cowherd, one called Tāmbūli is born—so we have heard.
From a merchant and a Śūdra maiden is born one named Kanduka;
from Kanduka and a Brāhmaṇa maiden was born Kaluṣāla.
From a Śūdra [beget upon women of the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa castes] are born the Āyogava, the Vaiṇa, and the Cāṇḍāla—the lowest of men; thus are the mixed castes (varṇasaṅkara) produced.

Sometimes the inferiority or superiority [of a result] arises from the greatness of the seed, and sometimes from the greatness of the field; yet the excellence [of the result] arises from both the field and the seed.
Sometimes, according to the natural order, caste is considered equal to that of the mother;
yet superiority or inferiority may arise from action, from time, and from qualities.
One born to a noble woman from a non-noble man may become noble through his qualities;
one born to a non-noble woman from a noble man is certainly non-noble. This is the settled rule.
From Kṛṣika, an Ambaṣṭha woman gave birth to Kuṭumbins;
and from Gopālī, a Kuṭumbin gave birth to a Kumbhakāra.
From a blacksmith, however, on a Karaṇī woman, one named Vardhaki is born;
from a Vardhaki, on a Tāmrakārī woman, one named Vāraki is born.
A potter (kumbhakāra) begets a palagaṇḍaka upon a Śūdra woman;
from a Śūdra man and a potter woman, a florist (mālākāra) is born.
Among girls purchased for a price, there are those of the servant class;
from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra girl, one born is known by the name Nāpita (the barber).
And from the mouths of those who were slain, there were born upon the fields Śūdras,
Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, Caṇḍālas, Kirātas, and other such tribes.
From a Kirāta woman and an ironworker, a blacksmith who sells weapons is born;
from a copper-smith woman and a weaver, a silk-weaver is produced.
A Vaiśya woman indeed gave birth to an Āyogava son from a Śūdra;
from a Kārāvara and a Kuvindā woman, one named Śauṇḍika is born. Furthermore, a son born of a Śauṇḍikī woman is a Raṅgājīva, and he is produced from a Vardhakī.
But because of the intermixture of castes, and due to both their mixing and non-mixing, this occurs again and again.
The infinite variety of castes that has come into being cannot be described in its entirety:
the Pauṇḍras, the Suhmas, the Palhvas, the Pulindas, and the Kinārayas.
The Kolas, Bhūṣārās, Varaṭās, Turkaṇas, Śabaras, Śakas, Pāradas, Daradas, Vyādhas, Niṣādas, and Pukkaśas—these are they. (Valc 2.19.27)
Those who speak Mleccha tongues and those who speak Ārya tongues are recorded as sixteen types of Dasyus.
The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the varuḍa,
the fisherman, the meda, and the bhilla— these seven are remembered as the outcastes (antyaja).
If water that has been left overnight in a vessel in the house of an outcaste is drunk,
one should indeed perform the expiation at that very moment.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Account of the Śūdra Class," in the Vallālacarita.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Henceforth, O lords of men, the Rudragītā is being told;
listen with focused attention to this eternal song.
Homage to you, O Rudra, for your fury, and also to your arrow;
homage to your two arms. I bow down to you, O Lord of the Mountains, O Ruler of the Hills.
O Rudra, O auspicious one, look upon us with that sinless, auspicious, and most peaceful form of yours, which, though terrible in appearance,
brings happiness.
O Giriśanta, that arrow which you carry in your hand for the purpose of praise—that, O Giritra, make auspicious; do not harm the person or the world.
Having heard our words with a gracious mind, O Lord Giriśa, speak so that this entire world may become well-disposed and free from disease.
The first divine physician, the supreme speaker, has spoken;
crushing all serpents and driving away the sorceresses.
To that copper-colored Āditya, who is also brown and most auspicious,
and to those Rudras who surround him in all directions— to them we offer our prayer for protection from wrath.
May he who approaches— the blue-necked, deep-red one—
who was seen even by the cowherd women, being seen, grant us mercy.
Homage be to the blue-necked, thousand-eyed, bountiful one!
Furthermore, there are those beings who have perished; to them I have offered salutation.
O Mādhava, loosen the two ends of the bowstring on both sides of your bow;
O Blessed One, cast away those arrows that are in your hand.
O you with matted hair, [withdraw] your divine bow, and be free of arrows while still possessing your quiver.
May his arrows vanish, and may he be one whose mind is fixed upon his quiver.
O most bountiful one, that weapon which is held in your hand, and that bow which you wield—let them not strike us; protect us from every side.
May the missile from your bow avoid us on every side;
and whatever arrow, O Rudra, you have in your quiver, place that far away from us.
Having drawn back the bow and shattered the tips of the arrows,
O thousand-eyed one with a hundred quivers, be gracious and well-disposed toward us.
Homage be to you, the weapon; homage to the bold one and to the one who is unstrung;
and homage be to you, the bow, with both your arms.
Do not slay our great ones, nor our small; do not slay our growing, nor our grown;
do not kill our father, nor our mother.
O Rudra, do not harm our beloved bodies.
Do not harm our children or grandchildren, nor our cattle and horses;
O wrathful one, do not slay our lives or our heroes—we invoke you.
Homage to the general of the army, the lord of the quarters; homage to the golden-armed one, to the trees with greenish-yellow hair, and to the lord of cattle.
Homage to the one who possesses the sound of the bowstring, to the radiant one, to the lord of paths;
homage to the thread-possessor, the golden-haired one, to the lord of nourishments.
Homage to Vabhluśa, homage to Vyādhi; homage to the Lord of Foods, and homage, homage to the weapon of Bhava and to the Lord of the worlds.
Homage to Rudra, the assailant; homage to the Lord of the Fields!
Homage to you, the slayer and the progenitor; homage to the Lord of the Forests!
Homage to Rohita, the master builder, the lord of trees;
homage to him who is the lord of the world and the one who bestows prosperity.
Homage indeed to the minister, to the merchant, and to the lord of the armpits;
homage to Ghoṣa, who cries out loudly, and to the lord of the foot soldiers.
Homage to him who runs, who is clothed in all things, the lord of beings!
Homage be to the victorious one; homage to the piercer; homage! Valc_2,20.23 //
Homage to you, the lord of the disease-free, the one with the crest, the quiver-bearer, the gliding one;
homage to you, the lord of thieves.
Homage to the Lord of the Forests, homage to Paricara; homage to you, the Lord of the Thieves, who deceives and utterly deceives.
I bow to you who possess a quiver; salutations to you, the bearer of the sword-case;
and again and again I bow to you, the lord of thieves.
Homage to those who carry spears, to those who desire to strike, to the lord of robbers; homage, repeated homage, to those who bear swords, to the lord of those who cut with axes.
Homage again and again to the Rudras who roam at night and run about;
homage to you, the turbaned one, the lord of the Kuluñcas.
Homage to those who carry bows and arrows, and to you who dwell in the mountains.
Homage, repeated homage, to those who stretch [the bow] and to those who fit the arrow to it! Valc 2.20.29.
Homage to those who draw back, homage to those who aim, and homage to those who release; homage to those who pierce, to those who sleep, and to those who wake—homage, homage!
Homage to you who are lying down, to you who are seated, and to you who are standing; homage to you who are the masters of the assembly, and repeated homage to the assemblies themselves.
Homage again and again to the mares and to the horse-lords; homage to those who are free from disease, and homage to those who pierce through; homage again and again to the fierce hosts.
Homage again and again to the throngs that strike down and to the hosts; homage again and again to the lords of the Gaṇas and the lords of the hosts. Valc_2,20.33 //
Homage again and again to the Gṛtsapatis, to the Gṛtsas, and to the Virūpas;
homage to those of universal forms, and homage again and again to the armies.
Homage, homage to you, the army commanders, the chariot-warriors, and those who are not chariot-warriors; homage, homage to the chamberlains, the charioteers, and the great ones.
Homage again and again to the young artisans, to the chariot-makers;
homage again and again to the smiths, to the potters, and to the Niṣādas.
Homage to you who are fowlers, to dog-keepers, and to hunters;
homage to dogs and to those who own dogs, and to Rudra and Bhava.
Homage to the blue-necked one, to the all-encompassing lord of animals;
homage to you, O dark-throated one, and homage indeed to you, the one with matted hair.
Salutations to you, the thousand-eyed one; salutations to you, the one with pervasive hair; to the wielder of a hundred bows, to Giriśa, and salutations to you, Śipiviṣṭa.
Homage to the most bountiful one, to the one possessing arrows, to the short, to the dwarf,
to the great, to the more vast, to the aged, and to the increaser.
Homage to the first, to the foremost, to the swift, and to the rapid; homage to the fleet, to the one who hastens, to the wave, and to the roaring one.
Homage to you, the river-born; repeated homage to you, the island-born.
Homage again and again to the eldest, to the youngest, and to the first-born.
Homage to you who are the middlemost, the unashamed, the one rooted in the depths, the one not born from another, the lowest, the gentle, and the one who wards off [evil]. Valc 2,20.47.
Homage to the one who belongs to the southern region, to the secure one, and to the one worthy of praise; homage again and again!
Homage be to you, the one belonging to the fertile field, to the one dwelling in the settlement, and to the one belonging to the threshing floor.
Homage to the one worthy of praise, to Kakṣya, and repeated homage to Śrava;
homage to Pratiśrava, and homage to you, Āśuṣeṇa. Valc 2.20.45.
And salutation to the one with the swift chariot, to the hero, and to the piercer;
to the one who is expansive, to the one clad in armor, to the one wearing mail, and to the one possessing a protective fender.
Homage again and again to Śruta, to Śrutasena, and to Dundubhi; homage again and again to Ahanya, to Dhṛṣṇu, and to Pramṛṣa.

Homage to the one with sharp arrows, to the wielder of weapons, to the one with his own weapon, and to the one with a good bow; homage, repeated homage, to the true one, to the one on the path, and to the one of the forest.
And salutations to you who are in the canals; repeated salutations to you who are in the small streams;
salutations again and again to you who are in the lakes, in the rivers, and in the ponds.
Salutations again and again to the one who is in the pit, to the one made of metal, and to the one who creates obstacles;
salutations again and again to the one who heats, to the pure, and to the one who exists in lightning.
Salutations again and again to the one who does not rain, to the one who rains, and to the one who consists of wind.
Homage to the Brātya, to Reṣman, to Vāstavya; homage, homage!
Homage again and again to Vāstupati, to Soma, and to Rudra;
homage again and again to Aruṇa, to Tāmra, and to Śaṅgu.
Homage to the fierce one, to the terrible one, to the foremost slayer; homage be to you! Homage to the one who strikes from afar, to the killer, and homage to the most deadly one.
Homage to you, the source of existence, the bringer of prosperity, the source of bliss;
homage to the doer of joy, the most auspicious one, and to Śiva himself.
Salutations to the one who is unobstructed and to the one who reaches the further shore;
salutations to the one who carries across and to the one who leads to the opposite bank; salutations again and again to the one who is bent.
Homage to the one who is in the young grass, to the one in the foam, to the one in the sand—homage again and again!
Homage to the one in the flowing stream, to the one on the pebbles, to the one in the dwelling place—homage again and again!
Homage to you, the desert, the path, and to Pulasti;
homage to the traveler, the cow-pen, and repeated homage to the bed.
Homage to you who are domestic, who are of the heart, and who are to be entered;
homage again and again to you who abide in the abyss, who are dry, and who are green.
Homage be to you, the dusty one, the one of passion, and the one who is to be erased;
homage again and again to the one who is to be wiped away, the one who is vast, and the all-encompassing one.
Homage to Parṇaśada, homage to Parṇa; homage to the one who strikes down, homage! Homage to the one who raises up, homage to the one who pulls out! Valc 2.20.60.
Homage to the makers of arrows and the makers of bows; homage to the one who digs up;
and repeated homage to the *kirika*s, the hearts of the gods.
Homage, homage to you who search and to you who destroy;
I bow again and again to you who have not yet been subdued.
O Lord of the blind, O clothed one, O poor one, O blue-and-red one:
do not fear us, nor injure us, in any way whatsoever—neither our progeny nor our cattle.
We offer these prayers to Rudra for his praise,
so that there may be well-being for all in the village— for both bipeds and quadrupeds.
O Rudra, that auspicious body of yours which is all-healing and the medicine of Rudra— O Rudra, with that, be gracious to us so that we may live.
May the weapon of Rudra avoid us on every side, and may the ill-will of the radiant one not fall upon us.
O Rudra, cause your firm [arrows] to descend so that there may be well-being for our children and grandchildren.
O most bountiful one, O most auspicious one, be gracious and well-disposed toward us;
O Śaṅkara, having laid aside your weapon upon the highest tree.
Wearing a skin and wielding the Pināka bow, may Śiva come;
homage to you, the Blessed One, Vikiridra-Vilohita!
May those thousands of missiles of yours cast us aside;
may those thousands upon thousands of missiles in your two arms [spare us].
O Blessed One, you are the lord of them; turn their faces away. Those thousands of Rudras who dwell upon the surface of the earth are beyond counting.
At a distance of a thousand yojanas from them, we unstring our bows;
for those who exist in this great intermediate space, in the ocean—
[we unstring our bows] at a distance of a thousand yojanas from them.
With blue necks and white throats, the Rudras have resorted to heaven.
At a distance of a thousand yojanas from them, we unstring our bows.
Blue-necked, white-throated, and dwelling below on the earth, those Śarvas—
we unstring our bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas from them.
Those who are tawny like young grass upon the trees, with blue necks and deep red [throats]—
at a distance of a thousand yojanas from them, we unstring our bows.
And those who are the lords of beings, the Viśikhas and the Kapardins—
for them we unstring our bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas.
The Āyuryudhas, who increase the lineage and who greatly guard the paths from demons—
of them we unstring the bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas.
And those who wander among the sacred fords, carrying spears in their hands and bearing quivers—
we unstring their bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas.
And those people who pierce others while they are drinking from vessels—
we cause their bows to fall even at a distance of a thousand yojanas.
And these many Rudras have spread throughout the directions;
we unstring our bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas from them.
Homage to the Rudras who abide in difficult places, whose arrows rain down;
for them, in all the cardinal and intermediate directions, I fashion ten fingers.
Homage be to them; may they protect us and grant us mercy.
We place that [power] in their jaws—those whom we hate and those who hate us.
Homage to those who dwell in the intermediate space, whose arrows are the wind; to them in all directions and intermediate points, I join my ten fingers in salutation.
Homage be to them; may they protect us and grant us mercy.
We place that [enemy] in their jaws whom we hate and whoever hates us.
Homage to the Rudras who are upon the earth, whose arrows are food;
for them who are in all directions and intermediate directions, I perform [this rite] with my ten fingers.
Homage be to them; may they protect us and grant us their favor. May they crush the jaws of him whom we hate and whoever hates us.
A person who recites, hears, or remembers this fierce song (gītā) of Rudra goes to the same world as Rudra and is not born again.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Rudragītā Upaniṣad of the Vyāsa Purāṇa, within the Vallālacarita.
Chapter Twenty-one. Siṃhagiri said:
O Vyāsa, O lord of men, this Purāṇa has been recounted to you just as the great sage Vyāsa formerly spoke it to the royal seers.
Enjoy pleasures as you desire, satisfy the ancestors and the gods,
and always gratify the Brahmins with various kinds of gifts, O lord of subjects.
O protector of the earth, perform the ancestral *piṇḍa* sacrifice together with your new queen, Śilādevī; a son shall be born to you through her.
And there, O scorcher of foes, O lord of the earth, perform the gift of the *tulāpuruṣa* at that sacrifice, remaining self-restrained after having practiced the *kṛcchra* penance.
May it be well with you; I shall depart toward the city of the Lord of the World, and I will return again whenever you remember me.
Śaraṇadatta said:
Having thus spoken to the king, O King, the sage Siṃhagiri then departed,
surrounded by those disciples with whom he had arrived.
When he had gone to Siṃhagiri, the king reflected for a moment in his mind,
and again and again he set his heart upon the piṇḍayajña and acts of charity.
Meditating upon the fruits of sacrifices and other rites, the king consulted with his minister, the domestic priest, Baladeva, and the brahmins.
Then, having consulted with the brahmins, the king at that time began to prepare the implements for performing sacrifices and acts of charity.
Then the king commanded his confidential minister,
who was endowed with all good qualities, regarding everything that was to be done in every respect.
The king said:
"Let all the materials be brought according to what was prescribed by the twice-born ones, such as Baladeva and others, as is appropriate for this sacrifice that has been inaugurated."
Haradāsa, Viṣṇudāsa, and Durgāsiṃha quickly [prepared] the provisions of food and other necessities, transporting them in carts in due order.
"Let the sacrificial enclosure be prepared, adorned with banners and other ornaments; and let the guest-houses for the high-souled kṣatriyas be constructed."
And let there be a hundred cooks and servers of food,
as well as lute-players singing and actors and dancers performing.
Let assembly halls be constructed for all the women of the inner apartments,
and let the noble classes of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras be invited.
"Furthermore, let shelters be constructed, well-provided with food and other necessities,
wherein Brahmins learned in the Vedas may dwell, duly honored.
Then the king, having summoned Lakṣmaṇa, spoke these words.
Go to the city of Vikrama and address him for the sake of the sacrifice.
"May my paternal uncle Śrīsukhasena and Prince Dhruva come, as well as all their retinues and inner apartments."
Śaraṇadatta said:
Having gone to Vikramapura, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes,
greeted him with joined palms and took his leave in comfort.
Dhruva and Sukhasena, having been joyfully and respectfully invited,
departed for Gauḍa for the sake of the sacrifice, taking the members of their harem with them.
Having heard of the sacrifice of Vallālasena, the Vedic twice-born who were experts in ritual then went to that sacrifice with joyful minds.
And brahmins, uninvited yet summoned by the sound of their own desires for wealth,
flocked from all directions by the hundreds and thousands.
The neighboring kings, accompanied by their followers, went forth on various vehicles, bringing gifts to enjoy the great festival.
The king’s officials provided them with many dwellings of beautiful appearance, well-stocked with various kinds of food and edibles.
Then, having seen Vallāla and being honored by him in return,
those lords of the provinces went to the dwellings as they had been assigned.
Then, having rested as they desired, the king, the princes,
and the others beheld that Pāṇḍava, the protector of subjects, seated in the assembly hall.
Then, at the proper time, the brahmins, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
initiated Vallāla, the son of Malhaṇa, as king.
The lord of the earth, having gone out to meet Sukhasena and Viṣṇumalla—
who were both worthy of salutation— paid them homage and spoke these words.
May Dharasena, Yajñasena, Dharmasiṃha,
and Dhruva likewise be gracious toward me in my sacrificial rites and acts of giving.
Having spoken thus, that righteous lord of the earth then appointed those officials to their respective offices according to their fitness.
He appointed Bhīmasena to oversee matters concerning food and drink,
and he appointed Bṛhaspati, the teacher of giving, to oversee matters concerning charity.
He appointed men to other offices as well,
and he told Lakṣmaṇa to take charge of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
The king’s sacrificial hall in Gauḍa was adorned with various trees;
it was radiant, provided with resting chambers, delightful, and beautiful in form.
It was adorned with various jewels, base metals and gems, variegated rugs, canopies, couches, banners, and flags.
Separate places were prepared for each of the groups:
for the Brāhmaṇas, the Kṣatriyas, the Vaiśyas, and those of the lowest birth.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, as well as the virtuous Śūdra castes [were seated there].
All of them, invited by the king, attained aesthetic delight (*rasa*) there in that *rāsa* dance.
The bhojakas, princes, kings, and nobles, as well as all the great provincial governors and high-ranking inner courtiers; Valc_2,21.37 //
Honored by Vallāla, they sat upon suitable seats in the assembly hall like the gods in heaven.
Shining in the midst of the assembly like Sutrāman in the Sudharmā hall,
the king performed sacrifices with the sin-destroying rite to the gods and the ancestors.
Then, equipped with a sword, wearing a turban, and adorned with all ornaments,
the king, desiring prosperity, performed acts of giving like another Karṇa.
There, with gold equal in measure to his own body,
he gratified the gods upon the earth with a gift accompanied by a thousand sacrificial fees.
Then, at the conclusion [of the ceremony], that king fed worthy Brahmins and others by the hundreds and thousands.
There, the gods and the ancestors became exceedingly well-satisfied by means of delightful *kavya* offerings;
and the classes of Brahmins were gratified by gifts of refined gold, edible foods and drinks, and abundant sacrificial fees.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Sacrificial Festival," in the *Vallālacarita* composed by Ānandabhaṭṭa, the son of Śaraṇa.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter:
"Then, on another occasion, the kinsmen and the family members gathered together."
The brave princes entered the dining hall.
When those great-souled ones had sat down upon their seats and were all eating with joy along with Vallāla, [the following occurred].
There, other groups of virtuous Śūdras entered the dining halls in emulation, so that no space remained for the Vaiśyas to see.
At that moment, the Vaiśyas, consulting with one another,
rose up, desiring to depart from the royal palace.
When some had gone outside or were preparing to depart,
Bhīmasena followed after them and spoke to them with humility:
"O great people, why are you departing without food?
Whatever intention you have toward us, you ought to speak it in every way."
Having heard that, the merchants said: "Listen, O noble sir!
Because of the contact with what was touched and what was untouched, we have become unable to eat. (Valc 2.22.7)
Disregarding them because Bhīmasena was exceedingly wrathful,
he cast them down, saying, "Such is the rivalry of Śūdras!
Then, there arose further disputes and counter-disputes as he became enraged.
Bhīmasena, the favorite of the king, spoke these harsh words.
Then all those merchants departed from the royal palace,
shouting and crying out like clouds at the end of the rainy season.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Merchant’s Humiliation," in the *Vallālacarita* as proclaimed by Ānandabhaṭṭa, composed by Śaraṇadatta.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Then, on another day, having approached the Lord of the Earth as he sat in his assembly hall—
Bhīma, the favorite of the king, spoke with his knee placed upon the ground.
"O King, all the groups of Śūdras have been satisfied with meals;
however, the gold-dealing merchants, out of pride, have departed without even eating."
Those merchants are exceedingly wicked, undisciplined, and arrogant of their lineage;
with evil intentions, they long for the food of the rows of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
Even though they had observed that the dining ground was devoid of low-caste people,
they disregarded the illustrious one and departed just as they had come.
O Great King, that evil-minded Vallabha, the leader of all the merchants, has been seized by the Pālas and is now in conflict with you.
His son-in-law is the lord of Magadha, Varṇamāna;
proud because of him, he considers the earth to be like a mere shallow bowl.
Having heard those words of Bhīmasena, the king then blazed with fury, just as fire blazes up by means of an oblation.
Grinding his teeth upon the royal throne,
that king shone like a thundering cloud risen in the sky.
From the head of that trembling body, his crown, radiant with diamonds,
fell like a mass of meteors from the sky at twilight.
At that moment, the king’s favorite, his eyes rolling with rage, [spoke].
He made a very solemn oath for the purpose of crushing the pride of the merchants.
The king said:

"If I do not cause those deceitful, gold-hued merchants to fall to the status of Śūdras, and if I do not inflict punishment upon the wicked-souled Vallabha-candra Saudāgi, [then let my head split into seven pieces]."

"Then whatever sins must arise from the slaughter of cows and Brahmins, those shall be mine. Just as Bhimasena has made his oath for the destruction of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, my oath for their downfall should be known to be of that same kind; until today, these have been treated like Śūdras at this sacrificial session."

Henceforth, the wearing of the sacrificial thread by these will be in vain; furthermore, those Brāhmaṇas who perform sacrifices for them, teach them, or accept gifts from them shall fall [into hell], even if they are blazing with merit—
there is no other way.
Before long, this proclamation was circulated throughout the kingdom;
hearing it, the merchants then gathered together and took counsel.
Because the king did not deliberate [upon their request], the resolute servants, their bodies trembling with rage,
blocked them from leaving the city of Gauḍa.
The Vaiśyas paid double or triple the price for their slaves;
due to the scarcity of slaves, great hardship arose among all castes.
When such great suffering had been reported by the groups of subjects,
the Lord of the World then reflected upon what ought to be done.
Seeing no other means at that time, he commanded the brahmins:
"Fishermen should be employed in menial services for the sake of the welfare of the world."
But the fishermen, desiring to enter into service, having heard the king’s command,
came to the royal palace by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Then the king spoke to them as they stood with their hands joined in reverence over their neck-cloths: "Service shall be provided for your livelihood; go and engage yourselves in trade."
Having made him the great provincial governor,
the king then dispatched Maheśa, who was even greater among them, to the southern border.
Then, on another occasion, garland-makers, potters, and smiths,
with hands ready and cloths bound around their necks, stood before the king.
Satisfied by their service, the king spoke these words:
"By my command, you shall be regarded as true Śūdras."
How is it that a king is not a deity, when by his word a man who is impure becomes pure, and one who is pure becomes truly impure? Valc_2,23.22 //
As time passed, the king caused the industrious servants to fall from their status as Brahmins— those wicked-minded wretches who were merely nominal Brahmins.
Appointed to his own service, he ran about busily;
and being pleased, he made that royal barber a *ṭhakkura*. Then, observing that the merchants were neglecting their own duties, he [proceeded].
The king commanded them all to abandon their sacrificial threads.
"Let the merchants living in the kingdom cast off their sacrificial threads;
he who does not cast them off shall be punished by the king"—thus did [the sage] instruct the servants.
Beating upon their drums, the servants proclaimed the king’s command in every city of the people, in the courtyards and along the streets.
Disregarding the king’s command and fearing for their dharma, the great multitude fled in haste toward all directions, taking along their wives and other attendants.
Some set out for Ayodhyā, others likewise for Mudgagiri; some went to Candramāyuta and Pāṭalī, and others to Tāmraliptī.
Some went to the city of Udaya, some to Mānagṛha,
some to the city of Vinīta, and others even to Śṛṅkhalā.
All those who had departed, tormented by the fear of the king's punishment,
cast aside their sacrificial threads, whether made of gold or woven silk.
At that time, having observed the family of Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas to be deeply distressed, Vallāla consulted with those learned in the Vedas.
Having distinguished the greatness of their seeds and then refining them,
that Lord established the states of Brahminhood and Kshatriyahood.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Deposition and Elevation of the Castes," in the *Vallālacarita* composed by Āndabhaṭṭa, as related by Śaraṇadatta.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter:
Formerly, the illustrious Rājavallāla was dwelling in the excellent city of Gauḍa.
Pṛthuprathas provided for the Arhats who were worthy of such honors.
Having caused a pleasant monastery to be built— divine, composed of baked bricks, with floors of variegated stone slabs, and furnished with beds and seats.
It was firmly founded, rich with painted halls, supported by sturdy pillars, and enchanting;
it featured fresh ivory pegs serving as supports for the books that had been deposited there.
It was adorned with delightful gardens filled with various flowers and fruits,
and possessed reservoirs of water endowed with exceedingly clear and sweet drinking water.
Equipped with doors and windows, furnished with various utensils,
plastered with lime, white in appearance, and filled with excellent food and other provisions.
It was adorned with places for exposition, meditation, fire-offerings, and recitation,
and was provided with dwellings for ascetics and travelers.
Accompanied by secret attendants, he formally presented the yogi Śrī Siṃhagiri in the presence of Pradyumneśvara according to the prescribed rite.
Likewise, endowed with faith, the king granted vast tracts of land for the procurement of items such as loincloths, fuel, and clothing.
Then that best of kings, whose intellect was purified by the excellence of all virtues and who was a subduer of adversaries,
had this edict engraved upon a copper plate.
The great king gave the village of Kāsāraka within Suvarṇamuktika to Anantaśarman Gautama for the increase of his merit.
It was provided with prepared foods and drinks, endowed with all kinds of grain,
accompanied by male and female slaves, and furnished with every utensil.
It was plastered with lime, very firm, secured with door-panels and bolts,
provided with auspicious entrances and exits, and adorned with lattices and other ornaments.
Having thus caused many such dwellings to be built,
the king then settled the Brahmins from the Deccan within them.
The lord of the earth performed the gift of gold, the gift of silver, the gift of cows,
and various other kinds of gifts, such as those obligatory and occasional.
As he enjoyed various pleasures and constantly gave gifts to worthy recipients, his time passed in happiness; no one has been his equal, nor will anyone ever be.
He did not fail to enjoy delightful pleasures that grant happiness, nor did he, as a wealthy man, fail to give gifts to those who were worthy.
By that [action], one obtains in the next world an excessive suffering that is harsh, terrible, and unbearable.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Performance of Dānavarman," in the *Vallālacarita* composed by Ānandabhaṭṭa.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter. Om, salutations to Śiva!
Golden-hued, beyond the darkness, the Golden Embryo, the inner soul of the world—the ancient Puruṣa was born from you; even the Vedas are from you. Be victorious, O God of gods! Valc_2,25.1 //
From you is born the progenitor of the world; you are the experiencer of all, yet you exist as the subtlest atom.
Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, O God Śambhu, whose form is bliss—victory to you!
You alone are Viṣṇu, you are the four-faced Brahmā; you alone are Rudra, the Lord Maheśvara;
you are the ether, Brahman, the void, and both the qualified and the unqualified.
Victory to you, O God, whose nature is pure consciousness alone! Sarva! Valc_2,25.3!
O Ekorudra, you create this universe here;
you protect the entire world which has the form of the universe; and in the end, this [universe] finds its dissolution in you alone.
We pay homage to Jayadeva, the primordial god!
Releasing streams of nectar, allay the suffering of gods and humans.
Indeed, the Vedas awaken you alone to the formless; be victorious, O Lord of the Universe! Valc_2,25.5 //
We bow our heads in homage to the Great Sage, the supreme Brahman, the purifier, the teacher of the world, who bestows resolute faith and liberation.
Victory to you, O self-existent god, Lord of the World!
You are the protector, you are the radiant one, you are the ultimate refuge, and you are the lord in the world; I bow down before you.
You are indeed the supreme physician, the remover of the arrow.
You are the physician; be victorious, O God of gods!
Stainless, pure, resembling a mountain of silver,
the bringer of an end to existence, the benefactor of the world,
and the bestower of the fivefold supreme eye of liberation.
We pay homage to the three-eyed one; victory to you, O God!
I bow to you, Śambhu, who possesses a thousand feet, eyes, and heads, who has a thousand arms, who is beyond the beyond, and who is the further shore of Brahman.
Victory to you, O God of gods, wielder of the Pināka bow!
I bow to you, Umādhava, the fierce one, the source of existence, the all-pervading Hara,
Kāla, Bhaga, and the maker of light.
Obeisance to the God who is the Self of all, Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Recitation of the Verses of Śrī Jayamaṅgala," written by Kālidāsa and Nandin, in the *Vallālacarita* proclaimed by the illustrious Ānandabhaṭṭa.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Then, having previously been exiled along with Dharmagiri by the Gaṇas—
Deprived of his livelihood, he traveled far, wandering from country to country.
Reflecting upon the humiliation and oppression inflicted by the king’s command,
as well as his own loss of office, Giri found no peace.
Then, after many years had passed while he contemplated the end of his enmity,
he beheld Vāyādumbara, the lord of the Mlecchas, surrounded by his own hosts.
Having raised up the wealth and jewels of Vallāla by means of a sale, he,
through his armies, besieged that city of the Mleccha lord at night with great valor.
Smoke-colored and wielding a bow like a cloud armed with lightning,
Vātāpi bellowed and leaped about in the midst of the army.
Grasping spades and axes, leaping with the great roar of waves,
and laughing with loud, boisterous laughter— that army appeared like the ocean.
Making the earth tremble with his footfalls and filling the ten directions with his roars of "huṃ," he caused the five-thousand-strong army of Mlecchas to dance.
Then the king, shrouded by the pleasures of enjoyment and dwelling in the midst of his inner apartments,
remained for a long time unaware of what had transpired until he finally awakened.
At dawn, having heard a great tumultuous clamor,
the king abandoned the vine-like arms of his beloved and then grasped his sword-blade.
Reflecting upon his city, which had its moats filled with unclean water and was devoid of defensive engines, the king considered himself already slain.
Then, seeing the king prepared for the expedition of war,
all the queens had their eyes clouded with tears.
Śilādevī, Padmākṣī, Subhagā, Hemamālikā, Sonadevā, and Caṇḍelī approached him and said:
"May there be no misfortune in this battle; may it be auspicious, even if the outcome be uncertain."
"O Protector, tell us, what shall we who are helpless and weak do?
Having heard those words of theirs, the king’s eyes became clouded with tears.
Having embraced them in succession and kissed their faces,
the lord of the earth spoke in return while gazing upon their lotus-like countenances.
A pair of pigeons is flying toward the battlefield of my beloveds;
if those two birds were to return like two returning monsoon clouds, [all would be well].
"Then you shall know our defeat on the field of battle,
O fair-faced ones! Your virtue as chaste women, which has been protected from the Yavanas,
my servants acting upon my command shall cause to be consumed by fire."
Having been addressed thus, and having embraced and kissed him again and again, he,
fully equipped and surrounded by his own forces, set out on his military expedition.
His military expedition, equipped with various weapons,
shone forth with elephant-riders, cavalrymen, chariot-warriors, and infantry;
thereafter, there occurred a great and tumultuous battle that brought about the destruction of the Mlecchas.
The surface of the earth was drenched with the blood of the hosts of warriors, both slain and those who had been struck down.
There, the king besieged the mighty Vāyādumba, whose strength was lost,
in battle, just as Śrī Rāma besieged Rāvaṇa.
Then, exerting his prowess with speed, the king, swift of hand,
severed his head just as Vāsava did that of Namuci.
When Jayashri, with a garland in her hand, chose the king,
then the servants of Yama bound Dumba with a garland in his hand.
At that time, due to the fault of their destiny, the two birds escaped from the cage;
or perhaps, having been released by someone, they reached the city of Rāmapāla.
There, seeing two pigeons approaching like two messengers of Yama,
all the king’s wives fell into a blazing fire-pit.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Supplemental History of Vallāla," in the *Vallālacarita* composed by the illustrious Ānandabhaṭṭa.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter:
Then, observing Piñjara to be empty on the battlefield, the lord of the earth...
Suspecting something utterly inauspicious, he turned back in haste.
Beholding the banner of fire from afar, he became extremely agitated;
then he entered his own residence to observe the total destruction.
Seeing his own wife half-burnt in the fire, Rummatta became utterly distraught;
though restrained with great effort by the people, the king threw himself into the blazing pit of fire.
In the Śaka year one thousand twenty-eight, O fortunate one, the lord of the earth ascended toward heaven together with his women.
In this regard, the teaching that has come down through the supreme lineage is heard:
Vallāla followed his father, who was distinguished by valor, in battle.
While a certain yogi firm in his vows was staying there in Mithilā, Vallāla,
during a military expedition, swiftly overran him.
Struck by the horse's hoof, the sage cursed Vallāla.
Accompanied by your wife, you shall fall into the fire-pit and die.
Remembering that curse of Brahmā, even though he had achieved victory,
he reflected in his mind as the time of his death approached.
Helpless by that very [curse], the king surely entered the blazing fire;
for without a Brahmin’s curse, such a calamity could not have occurred.
That lord of the earth was long ago destroyed by the Brahma-staff along with his wives;
moreover, the pigeon’s return and the king’s grief were not the primary causes of his death.
O King—may prosperity be yours—do you know that this auspicious pond of pure water proclaims the fame of one who has passed away, leaving only his reputation behind? (Valmiki Charita 2.27.1)
When the king’s fame had been destroyed by those who eat cows, and he himself became a sinner through the power of time,
it was as if he still existed through this [remaining] fame; alas, where has the lineage of the lords of the earth gone?

May this *Vallālarājacarita*, composed with great effort by the poet Ānandabhaṭṭa and endowed with the words issuing from the lotus-mouth of Vyāsa— shining like the new moon— cause the night-lotuses of the hearts of virtuous people to blossom.
Whatever has been stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa and whatever has been said by other wise scholars—
all that has been made manifest in this *Vallāla-rājacarita*.
As for the statement that "this earth has been made devoid of Brahmins by Subhūma," we consider that it was said out of fear of the king.
That was stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda either for the sake of sport,
or perhaps it might be irrelevant in the midst of the Vyāsa Purāṇa.
"In ancient times, this earth was rendered devoid of Kṣatriyas by the descendant of Bhṛgu;
for thus did the great sage Vyāsa himself declare in the Mahābhārata."

From a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya woman is born the Śūdra, who is called a Rājaputra; though of the same caste as gold, he is not eligible for the initiation ceremony, having fallen into the state of a Vrātya like merchants.
The cowherd, the garland-maker, the betel-seller, the brazier, the lute-player, the conch-blower, the potter, the smith, and the barber— these are the nine artisans.
The oil-presser, the perfumer, the physician, and the true Śūdras are thus proclaimed;
among all these true Śūdras, the scribe (kāyastha) is remembered as the most excellent.
The Gaṅgā, born from the foot of Viṣṇu, purifies the three worlds;
live for a hundred years, O Great King, who are born of her own lineage!
Whatever is most dear in the world, and whatever the mind delights in— dedicate all that to Acyuta and bestow it upon the brahmins.
